examples.everyday: I'm tired of all the rhetoric on the news; I just want to know what they will actually do.
examples.professional: Before we write the proposal, we should cut the marketing rhetoric and show the numbers.
examples.analytical: Aristotle treats rhetoric as a practical art that examines how speakers use logic, character, and emotion to persuade an audience.

nuance.analogy: Like the packaging around a product: it can help the product sell, but it is not the product itself.
nuance.etymology: From Greek rhētorikē (technē), the art of the orator, from rhētōr, speaker, orator.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the word with a hard, clearly pronounced t in American speech; the t is a flap, like a soft d.
Using 'rhetoric' only to mean 'argument'; in American speech it often suggests style over substance.

senses.definition: A deceased person whom a church or another religious group has officially recognized as especially holy or godly; one eminent for piety and virtue.
senses.example: The Roman Catholic Church proclaimed Kateri Tekakwitha a saint in 2012.

senses.definition: One of the blessed in heaven.
A Christian; a faithful believer in the present world.
A person with similarly overwhelming positive qualities; one who does good.
senses.example: Dorothy Day was a living saint.

senses.definition: Synonym of canonize: to honor, formally name, or revere as a saint.
senses.example: Many Catholics wished to see Pope John Paul II sainted immediately after his death.

core.definition: A person recognized by a church as especially holy, or in the New Testament, any believer in Christ.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable, rhymes with 'paint'. Don't add a vowel between the n and t. Before a name it is often reduced: 'Saint Paul' sounds like 'sunt PAWL' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it denotes holiness. Used jokingly, 'a saint' means very patient or kind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'saint' for officially recognized holy people (St. Francis) and informally for a kind, patient person ('You're a saint!'). Many cities and churches carry the abbreviation 'St.'. Protestants often use 'saint' for all believers.

distinctions.note: A martyr is someone killed for their faith; a saint need not have died that way.
A holy person is a general term; saint is a formal title or New Testament description.
Angels are spiritual beings; saints are human believers.

examples.everyday: You drove me to the airport at five in the morning? You're a saint!
examples.professional: The parish is named for St. Anne, the patron saint of mothers and grandmothers.
examples.analytical: Paul addresses the whole congregation as saints, which suggests holiness as a calling shared by all believers rather than an elite status.

nuance.analogy: Like a lighthouse: a life that points others toward God.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sanctus, 'holy,' via Old French saint.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the t in 'Saint' too strongly as 'sant-uh' or saying 'sent'.
Using it as an adjective in 'a saint person'; use 'saintly' instead.
Assuming all Christians use the word the same way.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew qadosh and Greek hagios mean 'holy, set apart.' In the New Testament, saints are all believers, as in Romans 1:7 ('called to be saints') and Ephesians 1:1, which address the churches. Psalm 16:3 speaks of the saints in the land as the excellent in whom the psalmist delights. Revelation 5:8 depicts the prayers of the saints offered before the Lamb.

traditions.view: Saints are those who died in grace and are in heaven. The Church canonizes them after investigation and a verified miracle, and honors them with feast days and requests for their prayers.
Saints are those whom the Church recognizes as glorified by God. They are honored, commemorated liturgically, and asked for prayers, with recognition arising from local veneration.

Many use 'saint' for all believers in Christ, as in Paul's letters, and do not formally canonize. Anglicans and Lutherans honor exemplary figures, while many others reject asking departed saints for prayers.

saint.etymology: From Middle English *saint*, *seint*, *sainct*, *seinct*, *sanct*, *senct*, partly from Old English *sanct* (“saint”) and confluence with Old French *saint*, *seinte* (Modern French *saint*); both from Latin *sānctus* (“holy, consecrated”, in Late Latin as…

senses.definition: The quality of being salubrious or invigorating.

core.definition: The quality of being healthful or pleasant for health, especially of a climate, air, or place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOO. The second syllable is a short, reduced vowel, so it sounds like brih, and the final -ty is a soft tee.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes healthfulness and is often used in praise of a place.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use salubrity in conversation. It appears in formal writing, real estate or travel descriptions, and historical or literary prose. For everyday speech, say 'healthy air' or 'a healthy place'.

distinctions.note: Healthfulness is the common everyday word, while salubrity is formal and rare.
Salubriousness is a near synonym but is even less common; salubrity is the more usual noun.

examples.everyday: People used to move to the coast for the salubrity of the sea air, and my grandmother still believes it.
examples.professional: In the proposal, we emphasized the salubrity of the site, since the hospital needed clean air and quiet grounds.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the moral claims about rural salubrity rested more on fashion than on any measurable health data.

nuance.analogy: Like the feeling of a cool, clean breeze after a stuffy room.
nuance.etymology: From Latin salubritas, healthfulness, from salubris, healthful.
common_mistakes: Using salubrity as an adjective; the adjective is salubrious.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel, as in brih-TEE instead of a reduced brih.

salubrity.etymology: From *salubrious* + *ity*, from Middle English *salubrite*, from Old French *salubrité*, from Latin *salūbritātem*, accusative of *salūbritās*.

senses.definition: A person or thing regarded as an agent of divine punishment.
A source of persistent (and often widespread) pain and suffering or trouble, such as a cruel ruler, disease, pestilence, or war.
senses.example: Graffiti is the scourge of building owners everywhere.

senses.definition: (historical) A whip, often made of leather and having multiple tails; a lash.
senses.example: He flogged him with a scourge.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To strike (a person, an animal, etc.) with a scourge (noun etymology 1 sense 1) or whip; to flog, to whip.
To drive, or force (a person, an animal, etc.) to move, with or as if with a scourge or whip.
To punish (a person, an animal, etc.); to chastise.
To cause (someone or something) persistent (and often widespread) pain and suffering or trouble; to afflict, to torment.

core.definition: A person, disease, or disaster that causes great and continuing suffering, or a whip used for punishment.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single stressed syllable, with a strong r and the j sound at the end. The silent-looking 'ge' is pronounced as the j sound, so don't add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes a destructive force or harsh punishment and is used in serious or dramatic contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'scourge' in news, history, and formal writing, such as 'the scourge of diabetes' or 'the scourge of war.' It sounds elevated in conversation and can come across as overly dramatic for ordinary problems. For everyday speech, people would usually say 'curse,' 'plague,' or 'menace.'

distinctions.note: 'Plague' often refers to a disease or widespread infestation, while 'scourge' emphasizes a force that punishes or strikes repeatedly.
'Menace' is a threat that might cause harm, while 'scourge' is an existing source of widespread suffering.

examples.everyday: Opioid addiction has been a real scourge in our town for years.
examples.professional: Our team has to address the scourge of duplicate records before we can trust the dashboard.
examples.analytical: Augustine treats sin as a scourge that human will cannot remove without grace.

nuance.analogy: A scourge is like a storm that keeps returning to the same coast, damaging everything it touches.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'escorge', from Latin 'excoriare' (to flay).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'SKOORJ' with a long 'oo' vowel.
Using it for minor irritations, which makes the word sound exaggerated.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is 'mastigoō' (to whip or scourge). In John 19:1, Pilate has Jesus scourged before his crucifixion. In Hebrews 12:6, the author quotes the idea that the Lord disciplines those he loves and chastises every son he receives, presenting suffering as a form of divine training.

senses.definition: The empty shell of a marine mollusk.
The animal living inside a seashell.
senses.example: The seashells on the beach are toxic and best avoided.

senses.definition: A very light pink color, like that of some seashells.
senses.example: seashell:

senses.definition: Of a very light pink color, like that of some seashells.
To collect seashells.

core.definition: The hard, empty outer shell of a sea animal, often found on beaches and sometimes collected as a souvenir.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the first syllable, and the second syllable has a light secondary stress. The sh sound is clear, and the final l is light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It evokes beaches, summer and childhood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say seashell for shells found on the beach, often in conversation about vacations or crafts. The word is common in everyday talk. Scientists or marine biologists may say 'mollusk shell' or 'bivalve shell' instead.

distinctions.note: Shell is the general word for any hard outer covering, while seashell specifically refers to one from the sea.
A conch is a particular large sea snail shell, while seashell is a general term for any sea shell.

examples.everyday: The kids spent the whole afternoon collecting seashells near the rocks.
examples.professional: The gift shop sells handmade jewelry using seashells sourced from sustainable fisheries.
examples.analytical: The spiral of a seashell is often cited as a natural example of logarithmic growth patterns.

nuance.analogy: A seashell is like a home a sea creature leaves behind, a hard curved room that holds a memory of the tide.
nuance.etymology: From sea and shell, from Old English scell.
common_mistakes: Writing sea shell as two words in formal writing; seashell is the standard one-word form.
Using seashell only for the living animal; it normally means the empty shell.

conversation.text: The kids filled a whole bucket with seashells.
I found a really pretty seashell near the water.
Let's look for seashells at low tide.

senses.definition: A ticket that is valid for all of the events in a series of related events for which individual tickets would otherwise be needed.
A ticket that is valid for multiple rides (limited by number of rides and/or time of travel) by public transit for which individual tickets would otherwise be needed.

core.definition: A pass that lets you attend all the games or events of a series, usually for a whole sports season, at a lower price.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of tickets. The second syllable of season is a reduced schwa with a syllabic n, and the final s of tickets is pronounced like a z or s with a light vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests loyalty, value and regular attendance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans buy season tickets for professional sports teams, theaters, and concert series. People say I have season tickets to mean they go to every home game. The phrase is common in American sports talk and business contexts such as ticket sales.

distinctions.note: Season tickets cover all home games in a season, while single-game tickets cover only one event.
A pass is a general term for access, while season tickets are specific admission for events.

examples.everyday: My brother has season tickets to the Cubs, so he goes to almost every home game.
examples.professional: Renewal of season tickets is our main revenue driver, so the sales team starts outreach in early spring.
examples.analytical: Season ticket packages function as a commitment device that binds fans to a team across an entire year of uncertain performance.

nuance.analogy: Season tickets are like a membership card for a club, giving you access to every meeting for a year.
nuance.etymology: Season is from Latin satio; ticket is from Old French estiquet, a label or note.
common_mistakes: Using season ticket in the singular when speaking about a plural set of tickets; Americans often say I have season tickets.
Confusing season tickets with a one-time event ticket.

conversation.text: My boss has season tickets and gave me two for Friday.
Season tickets are expensive, but you get the same seats every game.
We've had season tickets for the Packers for twenty years.

senses.definition: A straight line that intersects a curve at two or more points.
In a right triangle, the reciprocal of the cosine of an angle. Symbol: sec.
That cuts or divides.

core.definition: In a right triangle, the reciprocal of the cosine of an angle, or a line crossing a curve at two points.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the second syllable has a short a as in cat. The word is not pronounced sek-ant with an e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; purely technical.
nuance.usage_note: In American classrooms and math courses, secant appears in trigonometry and calculus, and students write it as sec. The trigonometric sense is the one most people learn first. Mathematicians also use secant for a line that cuts through a curve, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A tangent touches a curve at one point, while a secant crosses it at two or more points.
Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine, while secant is the reciprocal of cosine.

examples.everyday: My daughter asked what the secant button on her calculator does.
examples.professional: We used the secant line to approximate the slope between the two data points.
examples.analytical: The identity linking secant and tangent follows directly from the Pythagorean identity.

nuance.analogy: A secant is like a stick laid across a circle that cuts through it at two spots, rather than just touching it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin secare, to cut.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like sekant with an e vowel.
Confusing secant with the cosecant or cosine.

secant.etymology: From Latin *secāns*, present participle of *secō* (“to cut”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to the process of selection.
Choosy, fussy or discriminating when selecting.
senses.example: He's very selective and spent hours in the store choosing a new shirt.

senses.definition: Having the authority or capability to make a selection.
senses.example: In the USA, military conscription is controlled by the Selective Service.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the social work approach called selectivity.
Of or relating to natural selection.
senses.example: selective pressure

core.definition: Choosing carefully, or choosing only some items, people or options from a larger group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LEK. The first syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final -ive sounds like 'iv', not 'eeve'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use selective for careful choosing, as in 'selective about friends' or 'a selective college.' It can be neutral or slightly negative when someone is too picky, and context decides. In medicine and technology, selective is also used for targeted effects or processes.

distinctions.note: Choosy is informal and often mildly critical; selective is more neutral and formal.
Selected describes the result of choosing; selective describes a trait of the chooser or a process.

examples.everyday: I'm pretty selective about what I eat, so I usually skip the fried foods.
examples.professional: We need a selective approach to the data cleaning, focusing only on the fields that affect the forecast.
examples.analytical: Aquinas warned that a selective reading of the sources can distort our understanding of the tradition.

nuance.analogy: A selective person is like a good gardener who picks only the ripest fruit from the tree.
nuance.etymology: From Latin selectivus, from selectus, 'chosen', from seligere, 'to choose out'.
common_mistakes: Using selective with 'of' instead of 'about', as in 'selective of friends'.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'SEL' with an unreduced vowel.

senses.definition: (rare) Pertaining to the north; northern.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Relating to the north; northern. Used mostly in formal, literary or scientific writing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TEN, the second syllable. Keep the tri in 'tree' clear and reduce the final -al to a quick nul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a precise and somewhat old-fashioned word for north.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation; they say north or northern. You will see it in literature, poetry, historical writing and some scientific or geographic texts. Using it in everyday speech will sound stiff or showy.

distinctions.note: Northern is the everyday word for the direction or region; septentrional is more formal and literary and sounds deliberately elevated.
Boreal refers specifically to cold northern forests or climates, while septentrional simply means northern in direction or location.

examples.professional: The survey report divides the study area into southern and septentrional sectors for the field teams.
examples.analytical: The author's septentrional imagery links the cold northern landscape to the poem's theme of spiritual isolation.

nuance.analogy: Like a fancy invitation that says 'the north' when a regular letter would just say 'north'.
nuance.etymology: From Latin septentrionalis, from septentriones (the seven plow oxen, the Great Bear), applied to the north.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as sep-ten-TREE-uh-nul.
Using it in casual speech where 'north' or 'northern' is expected.
Confusing it with septuagint or other words starting with sept-.

septentrional.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *septentriōnālis*, from *septentriōnēs* (“seven plow oxen”), a name for the constellations now known as Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, which appear in the northern sky.

senses.definition: Likely to follow, conform, or yield to others, especially showing unthinking adherence to others' ideas; easily led.
Following logically or in an unvarying and orderly procession, tending in a single intellectual direction.
(poetic) Following neatly or smoothly.
senses.label: poetic

core.definition: Willing to follow others blindly; easily led, especially in ideas. Used in formal or literary writing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KWAY, the second syllable. The first and last syllables are short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests a lack of independent thought.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in speech; it appears in essays, criticism and formal writing about politics, culture or ideas. It is a sharp word, so using it about a friend or colleague can sound insulting. A more common word for the same idea is easily led or gullible.

distinctions.note: Gullible means easily tricked or deceived, while sequacious means readily following others' ideas or leadership.
A conformist adjusts to group norms, while sequacious suggests a more passive, unthinking acceptance of others' views.

examples.professional: The memo warned that a sequacious team would accept the first proposal without testing alternatives.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that a sequacious public becomes easy prey for demagogues who flatter its prejudices.

nuance.analogy: Like a duckling that follows the first moving object it sees, without checking where it is going.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sequax, sequacis (following, pursuing), from sequi (to follow).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with sequential or sequence, which describe order, not following others.
Using it as a neutral word; it is usually critical.
Stressing the wrong syllable as SEE-kwa-shus.

senses.definition: The state of being a slave; slavery; being forced to work for others or do their bidding without one's consent or against one's will, either in perpetuity or for a period of time over which one has little or no control.

A qualified beneficial interest severed or fragmented from the ownership of an inferior property and attached to a superior property or to some person other than the owner; the most common form is an easement.
(dated) Service rendered in the army or navy.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: The condition of being a slave or being forced to work for others against one's will, without freedom to refuse.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SUR-vuh. Americans often say the final syllable as 'tood' or 'tyood'; both are acceptable, but avoid stressing the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes a state of unfreedom, so using it lightly can sound dramatic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use servitude in historical, legal, literary, or serious moral discussions, such as about slavery or forced labor. In everyday speech it can sound exaggerated, so people often prefer words like 'drudgery' or 'grind'. It is common in civil rights and labor writing.

distinctions.note: Slavery names the institution of owning people, while servitude describes the broader condition of being bound to serve others.
Servitude is the state of being under someone's control, while servility is the eager, humiliating attitude a person may show.
Bondage can be literal or figurative, such as addiction, and often suggests being held captive; servitude focuses on forced service.

examples.everyday: My cousin jokes that being a parent is a kind of servitude, but he wouldn't trade it for anything.
examples.professional: Calling unpaid internships servitude sounds dramatic, but it does describe the power imbalance we should discuss.
examples.analytical: Locke ties freedom to the capacity to consent, which makes voluntary service sharply different from servitude imposed by force.

nuance.analogy: Servitude is like a rope tied to a person's ankle: the rope limits every step, even when the person has stopped struggling.
nuance.etymology: From Latin servitudo, from servus, meaning slave.
common_mistakes: Confusing servitude with servile, which describes an attitude rather than a condition.
Stressing the last syllable as in 'sur-vuh-TOOD'.

servitude.etymology: From Middle French *servitude*, from Latin *servitūdō*, from Latin *servus* (“slave”).

core.definition: A Hebrew personal name borne by several men in the Old Testament, most notably a royal official under King Zedekiah of Judah.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TY, the third syllable. The final -iah is a light, unstressed schwa-like vowel, not a long 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: You will mostly hear this name in Bible study, sermons or when reading Jeremiah and Ezra aloud. In everyday conversation you would rarely use it, but if a friend mentions him you can say something like 'Oh, the official in Jeremiah?' Americans typically pronounce it with a clear TY stress.

distinctions.note: Another Hebrew name beginning with Sh; they are different people in different books, so do not mix them up in discussion.

examples.everyday: Did you see that Shephatiah is in the Jeremiah reading this week?
examples.professional: Our study guide lists Shephatiah as one of the officials who pressed King Zedekiah to silence Jeremiah.
examples.analytical: Shephatiah son of Mattan appears among the officials who demanded Jeremiah's death, illustrating how court politics opposed the prophet's message.

nuance.analogy: Like a name on a list of council members: you recognize him by his role in one particular meeting.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Shephatyahu, meaning 'Yahweh has judged'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as 'she-FAT-ee-ah'.
Spelling it 'Shephatia' or dropping the final h sound in notes.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Shephatyahu (שְׁפַטְיָה), 'Yahweh has judged'. Jeremiah 38:1 names Shephatiah son of Mattan among the officials who urged King Zedekiah to put Jeremiah to death for his preaching. Ezra 2:4 records the family of Shephatiah, 372 members, returning from exile with Zerubbabel. These passages show him both as an opponent of a prophet and as the ancestor of a returning exile family.

core.definition: A Moabite town in Transjordan, east of the Jordan River, known in the Old Testament for its vineyards.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final ah is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'muh.' Don't pronounce the m as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Sibmah is used almost only in Bible study, sermons, and academic discussions of Moab and Transjordan. Americans would not use it in everyday talk. If you mention it, the context should make clear you mean the biblical place.

distinctions.note: Heshbon was a larger Moabite city in the same region, while Sibmah is mentioned alongside it as a place with vineyards.

examples.everyday: My friend reading Isaiah asked me about the vines of Sibmah, and I told her it was a Moabite town known for grapes.
examples.professional: In my lesson on the prophets' oracles against Moab, I pointed out that Sibmah was famous for its vines.
examples.analytical: The prophetic lament over the vines of Sibmah uses agricultural imagery to express the collapse of Moabite pride and prosperity.

nuance.analogy: Think of Sibmah as a wine-producing town on a regional map, mentioned when someone wants to describe the region's agricultural wealth.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, which is wrong for this name.
Adding an extra vowel between b and m.
nuance.biblical_note: Sibmah is a town in Moab, east of the Jordan, that appears in Numbers 32:38 among towns the Reubenites rebuilt or renamed. Isaiah 16:8-9 and Jeremiah 48:32 refer to the vines of Sibmah, showing that the town was known for its grapes. Prophets use the vines as a symbol of Moab's loss of prosperity.

senses.definition: Having no inverse.
Having the property that the matrix of coefficients of the new variables has a determinant equal to zero.
Not equal to its own cofinality.
Being only one of a larger population; single, individual.
senses.example: A singular experiment cannot be regarded as scientific proof of the existence of a phenomenon.

senses.definition: Being the only one of the kind; unique.
senses.example: She has a singular personality.

senses.definition: Distinguished by superiority: peerless, unmatched, eminent, exceptional, extraordinary.
senses.example: a man of singular gravity or attainments

senses.definition: Out of the ordinary; curious.
senses.example: It was very singular; I don't know why he did it.

senses.definition: Referring to only one thing or person.
Each; individual.
senses.example: to convey several parcels of land, all and singular

senses.definition: A form of a word that refers to only one person or thing.
That which is not general; a specific determinate instance.
A group of boars.

core.definition: Remarkable or unusual, or (in grammar) referring to just one person or thing; in mathematics, describing a square matrix whose determinant is zero, so it has no inverse.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Americans say the 'r' clearly at the end, and the middle syllable is weak, so avoid pronouncing it as a separate full syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In mathematics it is a precise, value-free term.
nuance.usage_note: In American mathematics and data science, 'singular' is the standard word for a matrix that cannot be inverted, which often causes numerical problems in regression. Outside technical contexts, Americans use the word for grammatical number or for something unusual, but the mathematical sense is specialized. Say 'singular matrix' rather than trying to explain it with 'no inverse.'

distinctions.note: Nonsingular is the mathematical opposite: a nonsingular matrix has a nonzero determinant and an inverse.
Invertible describes the same matrix from the other direction; a matrix is invertible exactly when it is not singular.

examples.everyday: My friend who teaches math said that some of the grids we were drawing were singular, which meant nothing to me.
examples.professional: The design matrix is singular because two features are perfectly correlated, so the regression coefficients are not identified.
examples.analytical: A singular matrix collapses the space it acts on, so no linear transformation can recover the original vector from its image.

nuance.analogy: A singular matrix is like a squeezed photograph: some information is lost, so you cannot restore the original picture.
nuance.etymology: From Latin singularis, meaning single or individual, from singulus, one each.
common_mistakes: Using singular to mean only or unique in ordinary sentences in technical settings, where the mathematical meaning is intended.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable as SING-gyoo-lar with a heavy 'yoo' that makes an extra beat.

singular.etymology: From Middle English *singuler*, from Old French, from Latin *singulāris* (“alone of its kind”), from Latin *singulus* (“single”).

senses.definition: Up to this point, all is OK.
senses.example: Well, you've packed your bags for the holiday, bought your tickets, reserved the hotel and put the dog in kennels. So far so good; now let's get to Minorca.

core.definition: Up to this point, everything is going well, though the outcome is not yet certain.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stresses fall on FAR and GOOD, while the two "so" words are lighter. In fast speech, the phrase flows together, sounding like "soh-fahr-soh-GOOD".

nuance.connotation: Positive, with a hint of caution because the outcome is not yet certain.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say "so far so good" in casual and workplace conversation to report that a project, trip, or plan is going well up to now. A natural reply is "Great, let's keep it up" or "Let me know if anything changes." It can sound a bit superstitious or hesitant if said about something very important, since it implies that trouble may still come.

distinctions.note: So far alone only means up to now; "so far so good" adds a judgment that things are going well.
All good is more relaxed and final; "so far so good" leaves room for future problems.

collocations: the test is going well, so far so good
the launch is on track, so far so good
so far so good, thanks for asking

examples.everyday: How's the new apartment? So far so good, except the heat takes a while to come on.
examples.professional: The migration to the new database is on schedule, so far so good, but we still need to test the rollback plan.
examples.analytical: So far so good, the argument holds, but it has not yet faced the strongest objections from the other side.

nuance.analogy: So far so good is like walking across a frozen lake: each step is safe up to now, but you still watch for the next crack.
common_mistakes: Dropping the middle "so" and saying "so far good"; the full phrase is more natural.
Using it for something that is already finished; it refers to progress that is still ongoing.

conversation.text: "How's the new job?" "So far so good."
The migration started an hour ago, and so far so good.
So far so good with the new puppy; no accidents yet.

senses.definition: To generate a linear span.
To extend across (a gap or space between two sides).
senses.example: The suspension bridge spanned the canyon.

senses.definition: To cover or extend over (an area or distance).
senses.example: The parking lot spans three acres.

senses.definition: To extend through (a period of time).
senses.example: The novel spans three centuries.

senses.definition: To measure by the span of the hand with the fingers extended, or with the fingers encompassing the object.
senses.example: to span a space or distance; to span a cylinder

senses.definition: To fetter; to hobble.
To be matched.
The full width of an open hand, from the end of the thumb to the end of the little finger, used as an informal unit of length.
Any of various traditional units of length approximating this distance; especially:
The English handspan, equivalent to 9 inches or 22.86 cm.
A small space or a brief moment of time.
senses.example: attention span

senses.definition: A segment or portion of space or time; a subsequence.
The time required to execute a parallel algorithm on an infinite number of processors.
A pair of horses or other animals driven or sold together; usually, such a pair of horses usually being similar in color, form, and action.
Ellipsis of linear span: a linear subspace generated by all linear combinations of a given subset of vectors of a given vector space.
Clipping of wingspan.
The spread or extent of an arch or between its abutments, or of a beam, girder, truss, roof, bridge, or the like, between supports.
The length of a cable, wire, rope, chain between two consecutive supports.
A rope having its ends made fast so that a purchase can be hooked to the bight; also, a rope made fast in the center so that both ends can be used.

core.definition: To extend across a distance or a period of time (the bridge spans the river); in linear algebra, to be the set of all linear combinations of a given set of vectors.

pronunciation.tip: Single syllable with a short a as in cat, followed by a clear n. Do not add a vowel before the final n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in mathematics and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians and data scientists use span as a verb or noun for the subspace generated by vectors, for example the span of a set of features. Everyday speakers use span for distance or time, so context signals the meaning. The mathematical sense is almost always used in lectures, textbooks and technical discussions.

distinctions.note: A basis is a linearly independent set that spans a space; a span is the set of all combinations, which may include redundant vectors.
Dimension counts the vectors in a basis; the span describes the whole subspace those vectors generate.

collocations: the span of a set of vectors
the column span of a matrix

examples.everyday: The bridge spans the whole river, so you can walk across it easily.
examples.professional: Before we fit the model, let's check whether our features span the feature space or whether some are redundant.
examples.analytical: A set of vectors spans a subspace precisely when every vector in that subspace can be written as a linear combination of them.

nuance.analogy: Think of span as the territory you can reach by walking in all the directions you have available: the reachable area is the span.
nuance.etymology: From Old English spannan, to stretch or fasten, related to spann, a hand's width.
common_mistakes: Using span as a count noun in math without context; in linear algebra it usually refers to a set or subspace, not a single vector.
Confusing span with spam or spin in pronunciation; keep the short a and final n.

senses.definition: The measurement of the wavelength of electromagnetic radiation, especially any of several techniques used to analyze the structure of molecules; the measurement of spectra of things other than radiation, such as the masses of molecules and their breakdown products.

core.definition: The scientific technique of measuring the intensity or wavelengths of light or particles to identify substances.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable 'trom'. The middle syllables are weak, and the final '-try' is a long 'ee' sound, so it sounds like 'tree'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise scientific term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'spectrometry' in chemistry, physics, and laboratory settings, often in combined forms like 'mass spectrometry.' It is rarely used in everyday speech. In talk with non-scientists, people usually say 'lab testing' or 'analysis.' The related word 'spectroscopy' is also common, and the two overlap but are not identical.

distinctions.note: Spectroscopy is the study of how light interacts with matter, while spectrometry is the measurement of the intensity or mass of the resulting signals.
Chromatography separates a mixture into its parts, while spectrometry identifies and measures the parts once they are separated.

examples.everyday: My sister works in a lab that does mass spectrometry on water samples, so she is always busy with testing.
examples.professional: We used mass spectrometry to confirm the compound's molecular weight before we scaled up the synthesis.
examples.analytical: Mass spectrometry reveals molecular structure only indirectly, so interpretation depends on assumptions about fragmentation patterns.

nuance.analogy: Spectrometry is like a sorting machine that weighs and identifies each grain of a mixture by its signature.
nuance.etymology: From spectrum and the Greek -metria, 'measurement.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'spectrometry' with 'spectroscopy' and using them as exact synonyms.
Stressing the first syllable (SPEK-trom-uh-tree) instead of the second.

senses.definition: A surface in three dimensions consisting of all points equidistant from a center.
The set of all points in three-dimensional Euclidean space (or n-dimensional space, in topology) that are a fixed distance from a fixed point.
An object which appears to be bounded by a sphere; a round object, a ball.
An area of activity for a planet; or by extension, an area of influence for a god, hero etc.
The region in which something or someone is active; one's province, domain.
senses.example: sphere of influence

senses.definition: The natural, normal, or proper place (of something).
senses.example: in one's sphere

senses.definition: A food preparation comprising a flavorful liquid treated by spherification to produce spheres.
(dated) The domain of reference of a proposition, subject, or predicate, or the totality of the particular subjects to which it applies.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (rare) The celestial sphere: the edge of the heavens, imagined as a hollow globe within which celestial bodies appear to be embedded.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (historical) Any of the concentric hollow transparent globes formerly believed to rotate around the Earth, and which carried the heavenly bodies; there were originally believed to be eight, and later nine and ten; friction between them was thought to cause a harmonious sound (the music of the spheres).
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To place in a sphere, or among the spheres; to ensphere.
To make round or spherical; to perfect.

core.definition: A perfectly round three-dimensional surface in which every point is the same distance from a fixed center point.

pronunciation.tip: Americans pronounce the r, so the word rhymes with 'fear' and 'near', not 'sfih'. Say it as one syllable with the vowel of 'fit' followed by a clear r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise technical term in math and science, and a common word in everyday talk about round objects.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people use 'sphere' for round objects like a globe or ball, but 'ball' is more casual. In math, 'sphere' means the surface only, while 'ball' means the solid space inside. The verb sense 'to ensphere' is literary and rarely used.

distinctions.note: A ball is a solid or round object used in games, while a sphere is the precise mathematical term for the round surface.
A globe is a sphere that represents the Earth or the sky, so it is a specific kind of sphere.
A circle is a two-dimensional shape, while a sphere is three-dimensional.

examples.everyday: That bouncy ball is almost a perfect sphere, so it rolls really far.
examples.professional: The sensor data can be modeled by points on a sphere, so we'll normalize the vectors before we compute the distances.
examples.analytical: A sphere in Euclidean space is the locus of all points at a fixed distance from a given center, and this definition grounds the classical theory of geodesics.

nuance.analogy: A sphere is like the skin of a balloon when it is fully inflated: all points on the surface are equally far from the center.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sphaera, from Greek sphaira, meaning ball or globe.
common_mistakes: Dropping the r, saying 'sfih' or 'sfee' instead of 'sfeer'.
Using 'sphere' and 'ball' as exact synonyms in mathematical contexts, where 'ball' means the solid interior.

sphere.etymology: From Middle English *spere*, from Old French *sphere*, from Late Latin *sphēra*, earlier Latin *sphaera* (“ball, globe, celestial sphere”), from Ancient Greek *σφαῖρα* (“ball, globe”), of unknown origin.

senses.definition: Rare and scattered in occurrence.
Exhibiting random behavior; patternless.
Not belonging to any infinite family; an exception to an otherwise orderly classification.

core.definition: Happening occasionally and irregularly, with gaps in between, rather than steadily or regularly.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, RAD. The first syllable is a weak 'uh,' and the final -ic is a short 'ik,' not 'eek.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sporadic in news, medicine, weather, and technical writing to describe events that come and go unpredictably, such as 'sporadic showers' or 'sporadic outages.' In casual speech people more often say 'on and off' or 'here and there.' It is neutral and rarely describes something pleasant, so it can sound stiff in chatty conversation.

distinctions.note: Intermittent suggests a repeating pattern of stopping and starting, while sporadic suggests no predictable pattern at all.
Occasional is milder and more everyday, meaning now and then; sporadic emphasizes irregular scattering and can imply unevenness.

examples.everyday: We've had sporadic rain all week, so I'm bringing an umbrella just in case.
examples.professional: The monitoring dashboard showed sporadic spikes in latency that didn't match any deployment schedule.
examples.analytical: Sporadic events resist simple causal explanation because their timing appears to lack any discernible pattern.

nuance.analogy: Like raindrops falling on a parking lot, each one lands at a random spot with no rhythm.
nuance.etymology: From Greek sporadikos, 'scattered,' from sporas, 'scattered seeds.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'SPOR-adic'; the stress is on -RAD.
Confusing it with 'sporadical,' which is an older and less common form.

sporadic.etymology: From Medieval Latin *sporadicus*, from Ancient Greek *σποραδικός*, from *σποράς* (“scattered, dispersed”), from *σπορά*, *σπόρος* (“a sowing [of seed]”).

senses.definition: A male steelworker.
A stronger version of an argument that one is about to critically analyze.
To repair flaws in an argument before analyzing it critically; to refute or to weaken the force of a stronger version of an argument than what was actually given.

core.definition: To restate an opposing argument in its strongest, most charitable form before you respond to it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, STEEL. The final syllable is a weak schwa, so say 'mun' rather than 'man'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals intellectual honesty and fairness, and it is praised in debate and online discussion culture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use steelman mostly in philosophy, debate, tech and online discussion circles. It is the opposite of strawman, which means attacking a weakened version of someone's view. A common phrase is 'Let me steelman your argument before I push back.' A natural reply is 'Fair, that is the strongest version of your point.'

distinctions.note: A strawman is a distorted, weakened version of an argument that is easy to knock down. Steelman is the opposite, presenting the strongest form of the argument.
Summarizing gives the main points briefly, but may be neutral. Steelmanning goes further by reconstructing the argument in its best form.

examples.everyday: Before we argue about the new schedule, let me steelman your view so I know I understand it.
examples.professional: Before we reject the proposal, let's steelman the team lead's case for using a simpler model.
examples.analytical: A careful critic will steelman the opponent's premises before showing where the inference fails.

nuance.analogy: Steelmanning is like testing a bridge with the heaviest truck you can find before you say it is safe.
nuance.etymology: Coined in modern debate culture by analogy with strawman; steel replaces straw to mean strong rather than weak.
common_mistakes: Using steelman as a noun meaning a steelworker; in logic it is a verb or a noun for the argument itself.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'man' instead of a reduced schwa.

senses.definition: Of weather: hot and windless and with high humidity, so that people feel sticky from sweating.
Tending to stick; able to adhere via the drying of a viscous substance.
senses.example: Is this tape sticky enough to stay on that surface?

senses.definition: Difficult, awkward.
senses.example: This is a sticky situation. We could be in this for weeks if we're not careful.

senses.definition: Of a death: unpleasant, grisly.
Mawkish, sentimental.
Tending to stay the same; resistant to change.
senses.example: a sticky price; sticky wages

senses.definition: Persistent.
senses.example: We should make the printing direction sticky so the user doesn't have to keep setting it.

senses.definition: Appearing on all virtual desktops.
Fixed at the top of the list of topics or threads so as to keep it in view.
Compelling enough to keep visitors from leaving.
senses.example: A woman has come to me with the complaint that her website is not sticky: 70% of the visits last 30 seconds or less.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of a stick.
senses.example: What's something that is brown and sticky? A stick

senses.definition: A sticky note, such as a post-it note.
senses.example: Her desk is covered with yellow stickies.

senses.definition: A discussion thread fixed at the top of the list of topics or threads so as to keep it in view.
A small adhesive particle found in wastepaper.
A sweet dessert wine.
Sticky-icky; marijuana, especially the sticky, resin-covered buds.
Wax.
To fix (a discussion thread) at the top of the list of topics or threads so as to keep it in view.

core.definition: Hot and humid, so you feel damp and uncomfortable from sweat; or tending to stick to surfaces.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -y is a light 'ee' sound. The middle t is a flap, so it sounds close to 'STIH-kee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes unpleasant conditions or messy surfaces.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'sticky' to describe humid summer weather, as in 'It's so sticky today'. It is also used for surfaces that are tacky, such as sticky floors or sticky fingers after a snack. In professional settings, 'sticky' can mean a problem that is awkward to resolve.

distinctions.note: Humid is a neutral, precise word for moisture in the air; sticky describes how that moisture makes you feel.
Muggy is a more informal word for warm, humid weather; sticky is more general and can describe surfaces too.

examples.everyday: It's so sticky outside that I want to stay in the air conditioning all afternoon.
examples.professional: The sticky part of the migration is the old schema, which has hidden dependencies nobody documented.
examples.analytical: Sticky questions about personal identity persist because they resist clean operational definitions.

nuance.analogy: Sticky weather is like wearing a damp towel: you cannot escape the warmth and moisture pressing on your skin.
nuance.etymology: From stick (Old English stician) plus the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using 'sticky' for weather without the stress shift; say 'STIK-ee' with the first syllable stressed.
Confusing 'sticky' as a verb with 'stick'; 'sticky' is the adjective form.

conversation.text: The rice is a little sticky.
My hands are sticky from the syrup.
These sticky buns from the bakery are amazing.
It's so hot and sticky out; I need a shower.
It gets sticky here in August, so pack light clothes.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being still.
Habitual silence or quiet; taciturnity.

core.definition: A state of complete calm, silence, or lack of movement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress on the first syllable. The -ness ending is a reduced schwa, so it is 'nuhs', not 'nes'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or peaceful; it can be calm and restful or tense, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stillness' in descriptions of nature, meditation, or a quiet room. It is natural in conversation, though 'quiet' or 'calm' is more common in everyday talk. In spiritual writing it can name a deliberate practice of inner quiet.

distinctions.note: Silence is the absence of sound; stillness can refer to lack of motion as well.
Calm describes a mood or weather; stillness focuses on the absence of movement or noise.

examples.everyday: I love the stillness of the lake early in the morning.
examples.professional: During the retreat, we used a few minutes of stillness before the planning session.
examples.analytical: In contemplative writing, stillness is not mere inactivity but an attentive openness to God.

nuance.analogy: Like the surface of a pond at dawn, stillness is calm with nothing disturbing it.
nuance.etymology: From still with the suffix -ness, forming a noun of state.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'stillness' with 'stiffness', which describes rigidity rather than calm.
Stressing the second syllable.

stillness.etymology: From Middle English *stilnesse*, from Old English *stilnes* (“stillness, quiet; absence of noise or disturbance, release, relaxation; silence, abstention from speech; absence of disturbance or molestation, tranquility, peace, security; that which…

senses.definition: Loud; shrill, piercing, high-pitched; rough-sounding.
senses.example: The trumpet sounded strident against the string orchestra.

senses.definition: Grating or obnoxious.
senses.example: The artist chose a strident mixture of colors.

senses.definition: Forceful (typically in a negative way) or obtrusive.
One of a class of s-like fricatives produced by an airstream directed at the upper teeth.

core.definition: Loud, harsh, and shrill in sound, or forcefully and aggressively insistent in opinion or tone.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, STRY, and the 'ent' ending reduces to 'nt' with a weak vowel, so the word is pronounced 'STRY-dunt'. The 'i' is a long i, as in 'sky'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes sound or opinion that is harsh, unpleasant, or aggressive in a way that makes listeners uncomfortable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'strident' mainly in writing, commentary, and political or cultural analysis. It describes voices, tones, or arguments that are loud, forceful, and unpleasant to hear. It can criticize someone's manner rather than their point, so use it carefully. In casual talk, people would more often say 'loud', 'harsh', or 'aggressive.'

distinctions.note: Loud describes volume only, while strident adds a sense of harshness or aggressive insistence.
Forceful can be neutral or positive about strong effort, while strident usually carries a negative judgment about harshness or excess.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's strident voice came through the wall, and I could not hear the TV at all.
examples.professional: The feedback in the review meeting was strident, so let's focus on the specific technical problems instead.
examples.analytical: The essay's strident rhetoric alienated readers who might otherwise have accepted its central argument about institutional bias.

nuance.analogy: A strident voice is like a smoke alarm going off in a quiet room: loud, sharp, and impossible to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From Latin stridere, meaning to creak or make a harsh sound.
common_mistakes: Using 'strident' as a simple synonym for 'strong', which misses its negative sense of harshness.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'stri-DENT', which is incorrect.

strident.etymology: From French *strident*, from Latin *strīdēns*, present active participle of *strīdō*.

senses.definition: An autonomous process that is launched by and communicates with another agent in order to handle part of the task that is the objective of that other agent.
A person employed by an agent to transact the whole, or a part, of the business entrusted to the latter.

core.definition: In AI, a smaller autonomous program launched by a main agent to handle one part of a larger task.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second syllable, AY, not the first. The final -ent is a reduced unstressed vowel, so say it as junt.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term used without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: In American tech teams, subagent is used mainly for multi-agent AI systems where one agent delegates work to others. In general business English, it refers to a person employed by an agent to handle part of a deal, such as a sub-agent for a real estate agent. A natural phrase in a meeting is the main agent calls a subagent to fetch the data, and a common reply is Right, so each one handles one piece.

distinctions.note: An agent is the main actor or program, while a subagent is delegated by it to handle one part of the work.
A subcontractor is a company or person hired to do part of a project, while a subagent in AI is a software process working under another agent.

examples.everyday: My phone's assistant hands the calendar job to a subagent, so I don't have to wait for it.
examples.professional: We'll have the planning agent spin up a subagent for the database queries and collect the results.
examples.analytical: A subagent's autonomy raises questions about how responsibility is traced when a delegated process causes an error.

nuance.analogy: A subagent is like a manager who hands one task to an assistant and then waits for the report before deciding the next step.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (SUB-ay-junt) instead of the second.
Confusing it with subcontractor, which means a company hired to perform part of a contract.

conversation.text: A subagent handles one focused part of the task in its own context and reports back a summary.
Using a subagent for the research keeps the main agent's context window clean.
Subagents can run in parallel, but the token costs add up quickly.

senses.definition: Placed in a lower class, rank, or position.
Submissive or inferior to, or controlled by authority.
Dependent on and either modifying or complementing the main clause.
senses.example: In the sentence “The barbecue finished before John arrived”, the subordinate clause “before John arrived” specifies the time of the main clause, “The barbecue finished”.

senses.definition: Descending in a regular series.
One who is subordinate.
A hyponym.
To make subservient or secondary.
To embed (a clause) into another clause that is the main one.
To make of lower priority in order of payment in bankruptcy.
To treat (someone) as of less value or importance.

core.definition: Lower in rank or importance than someone or something else; working under another's authority.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on BOR, the second syllable. The verb is pronounced with the same stress but ends in -ate, so the adjective and noun end in a reduced 'uht' while the verb ends in 'ayt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in organizational and grammatical contexts, but it can sound demeaning when describing people, because it implies a lower status.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subordinate for workplace reporting lines and in grammar, where a subordinate clause depends on a main clause. When talking about people at work, many prefer words like 'direct report', 'team member', or 'junior colleague'. In casual speech it can sound like you are looking down on someone.

distinctions.note: Junior refers to lower seniority or experience and is more common in everyday workplace talk, while subordinate emphasizes reporting to authority.
Inferior is a stronger and more judgmental word meaning lower in quality or worth, while subordinate describes a position in a structure.

examples.everyday: In our family, my younger sister gets treated as subordinate, which drives her crazy.
examples.professional: The data team is subordinate to product, so their priorities get set in the planning meetings.
examples.analytical: Aquinas argued that reason is subordinate to faith only in matters beyond its proper scope.

nuance.analogy: A subordinate is like a river tributary: it has its own flow, but it feeds into a larger river and follows its direction.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin subordinatus, from sub 'under' and ordinare 'to arrange'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as 'SUB-or-dinate', instead of 'suh-BOR-dih-nuht'.
Using subordinate as a noun for a 'helper' in casual speech, where people say 'employee' or 'team member' instead.

subordinate.etymology: From Middle English *subordinat*, from Medieval Latin *subōrdinātus*, past participle of *subordino*, from *sub-* + *ordino* (“to order”).

senses.definition: In excess of what is required or sufficient.
senses.example: With a full rain suit, carrying an umbrella may be superfluous.

core.definition: More than is needed or wanted; not necessary, and often a waste of time or resources.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root, PUR, so say soo-PUR-floo-us. The -ous ending is a reduced syllable, like us, not a full ohs.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying waste or that something is unnecessary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use superfluous in writing, meetings, and formal conversation to say something is unnecessary, such as "superfluous details" or "a superfluous step." It is more formal than "unnecessary" and sounds polished in professional contexts. In casual talk people usually say "not needed" or "way too much."

distinctions.note: Unnecessary is the common everyday word, while superfluous is more formal and often describes something that is extra on top of what is already enough.
Redundant means repeating what is already present, while superfluous means simply more than is needed.

examples.everyday: Honestly, the third appetizer was superfluous, since we were already full from the first two.
examples.professional: Let's cut the superfluous steps from the approval process so the release doesn't stall.
examples.analytical: The author argues that much of the theological apparatus is superfluous to the central claim about grace.

nuance.analogy: A superfluous word is like an extra spoon in a drawer that already holds enough: it takes up room without doing any work.
nuance.etymology: From Latin superfluus (overflowing), from super (above) and fluere (to flow).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with superficial, which means shallow or on the surface.
Mispronouncing the stress on the final syllable, as in soo-per-FLOO-us.

superfluous.etymology: From Middle English *superfluous*, from Latin *superfluus* (“superfluous”) + *-ous*, from *superfluō* (“overflow”), from *super* (“above, more than, over”) + *fluō* (“flow”).

senses.definition: The problem of how symbols in a system get their meaning from the real world rather than only from other symbols.

core.definition: The problem of how the symbols in an AI system get their meaning from the real world, not just from other symbols.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'SIM' and 'GROWN', and the 'ound' in 'grounding' sounds like 'ownd' with the 'd' nearly silent. The word 'symbol' is two syllables, 'SIM-bul', not 'sim-BO-ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in AI and cognitive science, used to describe an open problem.
nuance.usage_note: Researchers use it in papers, talks and debates about language models and robotics, often when asking whether a model truly understands anything. Americans say it as a fixed technical phrase and do not usually explain it to a general audience. In casual talk, people might say 'the meaning problem' instead.

distinctions.note: Symbol grounding is the specific AI version of the broader philosophical question of how words get meaning.
The Chinese room argument is a thought experiment about understanding; symbol grounding is the wider problem of connecting symbols to the world.

examples.everyday: My friend who works on AI says large language models still have a symbol grounding problem.
examples.professional: Our robotics team is testing whether the planner's labels for objects are tied to sensor data, which is the core of the symbol grounding question.
examples.analytical: The symbol grounding problem challenges the view that syntax alone can yield semantics, since symbols referring only to other symbols never touch the world.

nuance.analogy: Like a dictionary that defines every word using other words, with no word ever pointing at a real object.
nuance.etymology: 'Symbol' comes from Greek sumbolon, a token that was matched with another; 'grounding' comes from the idea of meaning being anchored to the ground of experience.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'grounding' with a clear 'd' sound, when Americans often make it sound like 'GROWN-ding'.
Thinking it means symbols that are physically written on the ground; it is a conceptual problem about meaning.

conversation.text: Symbol grounding is the problem of how symbols in a system get their meaning from the world.
Text-only training raises the symbol grounding question: does "red" mean anything to the model?
Robotics researchers argue that perception and action help with symbol grounding.

senses.definition: A sharp, hooked claw of a bird of prey or other predatory animal.
The shoulder of the bolt of a lock on which the key acts to shoot the bolt.
The remaining stock of undealt cards.
One of certain small prominences on the hind part of the face of an elephant's tooth.
A kind of moulding, concave at the bottom and convex at the top; an ogee. (When the concave part is at the top, it is called an inverted talon.)
(historical) A document that could be detached and presented in exchange for a block of further coupons on a bond, when the original block had been used up.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A sharp, curved claw on the foot of a bird of prey or other predatory animal, used for gripping and tearing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the second syllable to a schwa, so it sounds like 'TAL-un'. The 'a' is the short vowel in 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a physical feature of animals, though it can be used figuratively for a threatening grip.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'talon' mainly when describing birds of prey such as eagles, hawks, and owls, and sometimes figuratively for a fierce grip. In everyday speech people more often say 'claw' for cats and most other animals. The word is also used for the sharp part of a mechanism in technical contexts.

distinctions.note: 'Claw' is the general word for a sharp nail on most animals; 'talon' specifically refers to the claw of a bird of prey.
'Nail' is the flat or curved covering on human fingers; 'talon' is the hooked, sharp claw of a predator.

examples.everyday: We watched an eagle land on the fence with its talons spread wide.
examples.professional: The wildlife rehab center needs gloves designed to protect staff from the talons of injured hawks.
examples.analytical: The poet uses the image of a talon to suggest the predatory, merciless grip of power.

nuance.analogy: Like a hook on a fishing line, built to catch and hold.
nuance.etymology: From Old French talon, meaning heel, from Latin talus, meaning ankle or heel.
common_mistakes: Using 'talon' for the claws of ordinary pets; 'claw' is the normal word.
Pronouncing the first vowel as the 'ah' of 'father' instead of the short 'a' of 'cat'.

talon.etymology: From Middle English *talon*, *taloun*, from Old French *talon* (“heel, spur”), from Medieval Latin *tālōnem*, from **tālōnis*, from Latin *tālus* (“ankle”).

senses.definition: A video or voice call on Microsoft Teams.

core.definition: A voice or video call made through Microsoft Teams, the workplace app for chatting, meetings and calls.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'call' most strongly and keep 'Teams' a little lighter. The 'z' sound at the end of 'Teams' links smoothly into the 'k' of 'call'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical term for a common work activity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans, especially office workers, say 'Teams call' or 'Teams meeting' when the call runs on Microsoft Teams. Many companies use Zoom or Google Meet instead, so people often say 'Zoom call' or 'video call' in those workplaces. You might say 'Can you jump on a Teams call?' and the natural reply is 'Sure, give me two minutes.'

distinctions.note: Both are video calls, but a Zoom call uses the Zoom platform, which some American companies use instead of Teams.
A phone call uses a regular telephone line, while a Teams call runs over the internet within the Teams app.

collocations: hop on a quick Teams call
a Teams call with the client

examples.everyday: My mom wants to see the kids, so I'm setting up a quick Teams call for Sunday afternoon.
examples.professional: Let's move this discussion to a Teams call at two so we can share the dashboard on screen.
examples.analytical: A Teams call can flatten a difficult conversation, because the small faces and frozen frames remove many of the cues we rely on in person.

nuance.analogy: A Teams call is like a phone call with a window: you hear the voice and also see the faces, all inside the company's app.
nuance.etymology: 'Teams' comes from Microsoft Teams, a workplace app launched in 2017; 'call' comes from Old English ceallian.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Team call' without the s; the app's name is 'Teams'.
Using 'Teams call' for any video call; in many American offices it means only a call on that particular app.

conversation.text: I'm on a Teams call until three, so text me.
Can you set up a Teams call with the vendor for tomorrow?
My Teams call froze, so I rejoined from my phone.

senses.definition: A type of argument for the existence of God, stating that orderliness of nature is evidence of design, therefore also of a designer.

core.definition: An argument for God's existence holding that the order and purposefulness of nature is evidence of design, and therefore of a designer. Also called the argument from design.

pronunciation.tip: Argument has stress on the first syllable, and the -gu- is quick, so say AR-gyuh-muhnt.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical label used in philosophy and theology classes, and it is neither praise nor criticism of the argument.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in philosophy of religion courses, theology, and debates about intelligent design. It is formal and precise, so use it in academic or serious discussion rather than casual conversation. In everyday talk, people more often say argument from design.

distinctions.note: The ontological argument infers God's existence from the concept of God alone, while the teleological argument infers a designer from observed order in nature.
The cosmological argument reasons from the existence of the universe or its causes, while the teleological argument reasons from the purposeful structure of nature.

examples.everyday: My friend says the beauty of nature proves God made it, which is basically the teleological argument.
examples.professional: In the seminar, our instructor asked us to outline the teleological argument before we discussed its weaknesses.
examples.analytical: Hume's critique of the teleological argument targets the analogy between natural order and human artifacts, questioning whether we can infer a designer from the world's apparent purposiveness.

nuance.analogy: It is like finding a watch on a beach and concluding that someone must have made it, because its parts clearly work together toward a purpose.
nuance.etymology: From Greek telos (end, purpose) and -logical, from logos (reason, study).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in teleological, saying tee-lee-uh-LAH-jih-kuhl with the main stress in the right place but mispronouncing the -gi- sound as a hard g.
Using the term to mean any argument about design, when it specifically refers to an argument for a designer of the universe.

senses.definition: Moderation or self-control in any action; control of the desire to act emotionally; calmness; an instance of this.
(Habitual) moderation in regard to the indulgence of natural appetites and passions; moderate or restrained indulgence.
senses.example: temperance in eating and drinking

senses.definition: Moderation in the use of intoxicating substances; sobriety; specifically, complete abstinence from alcoholic beverages; teetotalism.
Synonym of chastity (“abstinence from any sexual activity considered immoral”).
The action of bringing to a temperate or moderate state.
Proper moderation between extreme or opposing qualities; an instance of this.
Temperature which is neither too cold nor too hot.
(dated) Restraint or self-control when made angry or frustrated; forbearance.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Advocating or practising complete abstinence from alcoholic beverages.

core.definition: Moderation and self-control, especially in eating, drinking, and the indulgence of desires and pleasures.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the -ance ending is reduced to a weak 'uhnts' sound, not a full 'ants'. The first two syllables may blend, so keep the 'p' light.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises self-control and balance, though in American history it is also linked with the temperance movement against alcohol.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use temperance mainly in religious, moral, or historical contexts, and it can sound old-fashioned in casual speech. In the United States, temperance often means abstaining from alcohol because of the nineteenth-century temperance movement. In everyday talk, people usually say moderation or self-control instead.

distinctions.note: Moderation is the everyday term for not overdoing something, while temperance is a more formal moral virtue of self-restraint.
Abstinence means giving something up completely, while temperance can mean balanced use rather than total avoidance, though American usage often narrows it to alcohol.
Self-control is the general everyday term for restraint, while temperance is more formal and often used in discussions of virtue.

examples.everyday: My grandfather believed in temperance, so he never had more than one beer at a barbecue.
examples.professional: Our wellness program encourages temperance with holiday snacks and alcohol at team events, without banning either.
examples.analytical: Aquinas treats temperance as the cardinal virtue that moderates the pleasures of touch and taste, so that appetite serves reason.

nuance.analogy: Temperance is like a good thermostat for the appetites: it keeps the heat of desire at a comfortable level rather than letting it overheat or go cold.
nuance.etymology: From Latin temperantia, meaning moderation or self-restraint, from temperare.
common_mistakes: Using temperance as a general word for cheapness or thrift; it means moderation in indulgence.
Saying a person has a temperance when the natural form is a person of temperance or practices temperance.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the idea appears as self-control rather than the word temperance in the RSV. The Greek word is enkrateia, meaning self-mastery or control over one's desires. Galatians 5:23 lists self-control among the fruit of the Spirit, which describes restraint over bodily appetites as the work of God in a believer. Acts 24:25 records Paul speaking to Felix about righteousness, self-control, and future judgment, where the same Greek idea is used. 2 Peter 1:6 includes self-control in a list of virtues that believers are to add to their faith.

temperance.etymology: The is derived from Middle English *temperaunce* (“forbearance, restraint; moderation, temperateness; gentleness, modesty; action of achieving a compromise between two extremes; etc.”), from Anglo-Norman *temperaunce*, from Latin *temperantia*…

senses.definition: The act of tempting.
The condition of being tempted.
Something attractive, tempting or seductive; an inducement, seducement, or enticement.
Pressure applied to one's thinking designed to create wrong emotions which will eventually lead to wrong actions.

core.definition: A strong desire to do something you know you should avoid, or something that attracts you toward it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TAY, and the p is pronounced, not silent. The ending is 'shun', not 'shee-un'.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it usually suggests something you should resist, though playful speech can use it for tempting treats, as in 'that cake is a temptation'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say resist temptation or give in to temptation, especially in everyday moral talk and in church. In casual speech they also say a treat is a temptation when they want to eat it. A natural reply to a tempting offer is 'Oh, you're tempting me!'

distinctions.note: An urge is a sudden impulse that is not necessarily wrong. A temptation is attractive precisely because it pulls you toward something you should avoid.
A craving is a strong physical or emotional desire, such as for sweets. Temptation involves a choice between what you want and what you should do.
Allure is the charm or appeal of something, often positive. Temptation implies a pull toward a choice that may be wrong.

examples.everyday: I know I shouldn't, but that donut in the break room is too much of a temptation.
examples.professional: The temptation to ship the feature before testing is strong, so let's add a checklist to the release process.
examples.analytical: Moral philosophy has long asked why the temptation to deceive seems strongest when deception appears to cost nothing.

nuance.analogy: Temptation is like a magnet placed near a compass: it pulls hard even when you are trying to point somewhere else.
nuance.etymology: From Latin temptatio, from temptare 'to try, test, tempt'.
common_mistakes: Dropping the p in pronunciation; say 'temp-TAY-shun' with a clear p.
Saying 'I have a temptation' where 'I feel tempted' is more natural.
Using temptation for a simple choice; it implies a pull toward something you should avoid.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word peirasmos can mean testing, trial or temptation, depending on context. In Matthew 4:1 Jesus is led into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil, and James 1:13-14 says that God tempts no one and that each person is drawn away by his own desire. In 1 Corinthians 10:13 Paul says that no temptation has overtaken believers beyond what is common to humanity, and that God provides a way of escape. The Lord's Prayer in Matthew 6:13 asks God not to lead us into temptation.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of text message, a brief written message transmitted between mobile phones.
A writing consisting of multiple glyphs, characters, symbols or sentences.
A book, tome or other set of writings.
Anything chosen as the subject of an argument, literary composition, etc.
Data which can be interpreted as human-readable text.
A verse or passage of Scripture, especially one chosen as the subject of a sermon, or in proof of a doctrine.
A style of writing in large characters; also, a kind of type used in printing.
senses.example: German text

senses.definition: To send a text message to; i.e. to transmit text using the Short Message Service (SMS), or a similar service, between communications devices, particularly mobile phones.
senses.example: Just text me when you get here.

senses.definition: To send and receive text messages.
senses.example: Have you been texting all afternoon?

senses.definition: (dated) To write in large characters, as in text hand.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A short written message sent electronically from one mobile phone to another.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one syllable with a short e and a clean final cluster, /kst/. Do not add a vowel after the x sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and casual. In formal writing, people say 'message' or 'letter' instead.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use text as a noun for a text message ('I got a text from her') and as a verb ('text me when you land'). In professional settings, a quick text is fine for logistics, but anything substantive usually goes by email. The sense of written words in a book is separate and more formal.

distinctions.note: Message is general and can be spoken or written; text specifically means a typed message sent by phone.
Email goes through an email system and is usually longer and more formal than a text.

examples.everyday: Hey, can you send me a text when you get home?
examples.professional: I'll send you a text if the meeting moves to three o'clock.
examples.analytical: Studies of how teenagers coordinate plans by text show that very short messages can carry a surprising amount of social meaning.

nuance.analogy: A text is a postcard for your phone: short, quick and sent without the formality of a letter.
nuance.etymology: From Latin textus, 'woven thing', from texere, 'to weave'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'text to him' instead of 'text him' or 'send him a text'.
Confusing text (a message) with textbook or texture.

conversation.text: Text me when you get home.
I got a text from the bank saying my card was used.
The text on this slide is too small to read.

senses.definition: Lacking in courage or confidence.
senses.example: John's a very timid person. I doubt he'll be brave enough to face his brother.

core.definition: Easily frightened or shy, lacking courage or self-confidence in ordinary situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the i in both syllables is short, as in 'bit.' The word does not rhyme with 'tie-mid,' which is a common learner error.

nuance.connotation: Negative to mildly negative; it describes a personality trait, though a gentle timid person may be described kindly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use timid for people who hesitate to speak up, try new things, or take risks. Saying someone is timid is a fairly direct judgment, so use it carefully about colleagues. For a shy person, people often say shy or reserved.

distinctions.note: Shy describes discomfort around other people, while timid describes a general lack of courage to act or speak.
Cautious suggests careful, reasoned prudence, while timid suggests fear that holds someone back.

examples.everyday: She gave a timid knock on the door, not sure anyone was home.
examples.professional: Our junior engineers were too timid to challenge the roadmap in meetings, so the risks went unspoken.
examples.analytical: The author describes the timid reader as one who avoids hard texts, which turns intellectual caution into a moral failing.
