nuance.analogy: Timid is like a turtle that pulls its head in at the first noise: it is not stupid, just too afraid to move forward.
nuance.etymology: From Latin timidus, from timere, to fear.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long i, as in 'TIE-mid'.
Using timid when shy is more accurate for someone who is socially uncomfortable but confident in their work.

timid.etymology: From Middle French *timide*, from Latin *timidus* (“full of fear, fearful, timid”), from *timeō* (“to fear”).

senses.definition: Of, relating to, being, derived from, or having a title.
Existing in name only; nominal.
Named or referred to in the title.
senses.example: Macbeth is a titular character.

senses.definition: One who holds a title.
The person from whom a church takes its special name; distinguished from a patron, who must be canonized or an angel.

core.definition: Existing in name only; holding a title or position without real power or duties.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle sound is 'ch', as in 'church', and the last syllable is a reduced, rhotic 'er'. Do not say 'TIT-yoo-lar'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative when describing a leader who lacks real authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use titular in news, politics, and business to describe someone who has a title but little real power, such as a titular head of state. In casual speech people more often say figurehead or in name only. Using it in a conversation with friends can sound formal, but it is natural in analysis and journalism.

distinctions.note: Nominal stresses that something exists in name or on paper, while titular stresses that someone holds a title with no real authority.
Honorary describes a title given as a tribute, often without duties, while titular describes a title that exists without real power in practice.

examples.everyday: My uncle is the titular president of the club, but his daughter actually runs everything.
examples.professional: The board named her the titular chair, while the operating decisions went to the CEO.
examples.analytical: The constitution made the monarch the titular head of state, leaving the real power of government with elected officials.

nuance.analogy: A titular leader is like a flag on a building: it marks the place and carries a name, but it does not run the building.
nuance.etymology: From Latin titulus, 'title, inscription'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'TIT-yoo-lar' with a 'yoo' sound, which is not standard American.
Confusing titular with entitled, which means having a right to something.

titular.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *titulaire*, from Latin *titulāris*, from *titulus* (“title”).

senses.definition: A system that parses an input stream into its component tokens.

core.definition: A program or component that splits an input stream, such as text, into the tokens a computer will process.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the middle syllables light. The final -er is an American r-colored vowel, so say 'zer' with the r clearly heard, not 'zuh' or 'zah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a neutral technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tokenizer for a specific tool, such as the component that comes with a language model or a library. People often say 'the tokenizer' to mean the tool attached to a model. Compiler engineers may say lexer instead.

distinctions.note: A lexer is a lexical analyzer from compiler design, while tokenizer is the more general term used in machine learning and text processing.
A tokenizer breaks input into units, while a parser builds a structure from those units.

examples.everyday: The app uses the same tokenizer as the model, so the word counts match.
examples.professional: We need to update the tokenizer before deploying the new model, or the vocabulary won't match.
examples.analytical: A tokenizer embeds assumptions about what counts as a word, and those assumptions shape the model's behavior across languages.

nuance.analogy: Like a sorting machine at a post office that places each letter into its own bin.
nuance.etymology: From tokenize plus the agent suffix -er; token is from Old English tācen, sign.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'toh-kuh-NY-zer'.
Dropping the final r, so it sounds like 'tokenize-uh'.

conversation.text: The tokenizer converts raw text into integer IDs from a fixed vocabulary before the model sees anything.
Some of the arithmetic errors came from the tokenizer splitting long numbers into odd chunks.
Many tokenizers are less efficient on languages like Amharic, so the same sentence takes far more tokens than in English.

senses.definition: Appearing to be exceptionally good, and therefore arousing suspicion of illegitimacy.
senses.example: He wants to give you two million dollars? That's just too good to be true!

core.definition: Seeming so favorable that it is probably false, unrealistic, or a scam.

pronunciation.tip: Reduce 'to' to 'tuh' or 'tu' in speech, and make 'be' short as 'bee'. The r in 'true' is strong in General American.

nuance.connotation: Negative or cautious. It signals suspicion, and it can suggest that someone should check the facts before trusting an offer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when a deal, offer, or story sounds too favorable to trust, often in shopping, investing, or online messages. It is a warning, not praise. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I thought the same thing' or 'Let's check it out first'.

distinctions.note: Sounds fishy is more informal and suggests something is suspicious, while too good to be true focuses on the offer being unrealistically favorable.
Unbelievable can be a compliment or an exclamation, while too good to be true is a warning about deception.

collocations: sounds too good to be true
a deal too good to be true
that's too good to be true
seemed too good to be true
an offer too good to be true

examples.everyday: A guy on the street offered me a new phone for fifty bucks, but it sounded too good to be true.
examples.professional: The vendor promised a forty percent cost cut with no downtime, which is too good to be true, so let's pilot it first.
examples.analytical: A proposal that promises certainty without cost is often too good to be true, and philosophers have long been wary of such claims.

nuance.analogy: It is like a sign in a shop window that says everything is free: you check the fine print before you believe it.
common_mistakes: Using it as praise for something very impressive, when it actually signals suspicion.
Saying 'too good to be true' without the final 'true' sound, which is part of the idiom.

conversation.text: A free cruise? That sounds too good to be true.
The job offer seemed too good to be true, and it was a scam.
If the results look too good to be true, check the data again.

senses.definition: In AI: In reinforcement learning, the sequence of states, actions and rewards in one episode.
The path an object takes as it moves.
The ordered set of intermediate states assumed by a dynamical system as a result of time evolution.
A course of development, such as that of a war or career.
The path of a body as it travels through space.

core.definition: The path an object follows through the air or space, or the course of development over time (a career trajectory); in reinforcement learning, the sequence of states, actions and rewards an agent experiences in one episode.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, JEK. The first syllable is weak, so say 'truh' rather than 'tra', and the final -ory is a quick 'uh-ree'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a path or pattern without judging whether it is good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: In data science and AI, trajectory usually means the recorded path of an episode or a sequence of states. In everyday American speech it means the general direction of something over time, such as a career or a company's trajectory. A common phrase in meetings is 'if we stay on this trajectory,' meaning 'if things continue this way.'

distinctions.note: Path is general and neutral; trajectory emphasizes a course that follows a measurable or predictable pattern over time.
Course is everyday for a direction or plan; trajectory suggests a pattern you can plot and extend into the future.
In reinforcement learning an episode is one complete run, while a trajectory is the recorded sequence of states, actions, and rewards within that episode.

examples.everyday: Our sales are on a good trajectory this year, so I'm not worried.
examples.professional: The debugging script logs every agent trajectory so we can see where the policy starts to go wrong.
examples.analytical: Each trajectory in the training batch is a sample from the policy's distribution over state-action sequences, which determines the variance of the gradient estimate.

nuance.analogy: A trajectory is like a GPS breadcrumb trail: each point records where you were and what you did, so the whole route is visible.
nuance.etymology: From Neo-Latin trajectoria, from Latin trajicere, 'to throw across', from trans-, across, and jacere, 'to throw'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable or saying 'TRAJ-ik-tor-ee' with a hard j and long a; the stress is on JEK.
Using trajectory for a single static position; it implies movement over time.

trajectory.etymology: From New Latin *trāiectōria* (“trajectory”), the feminine of *trāiectōrius* (“of or pertaining to throwing across”), from Latin *trāiectus* (“thrown over or across”), past participle of *trāiciō*, from *trans-* (“across, beyond”) (see *trans-*) + *iaciō*…

conversation.text: A trajectory is the sequence of states, actions, and rewards from one run of the policy.
We reviewed failed agent trajectories to see where the plan went wrong.
Her career trajectory changed when she moved from analytics into machine learning.

senses.definition: To exceed or overstep some limit or boundary.
To act in violation of some law.
To commit an offense; to sin.
To spread over land along a shoreline; to inundate.

core.definition: To break a rule, law, or moral principle, or to go beyond a limit that someone has set or that is considered acceptable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, GRES. The 'ns' cluster is pronounced as 'nz' here, so say 'tranz', not 'trans', before the 'g'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies breaking a rule, law or boundary, often with a sense of moral wrongdoing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'transgress' in formal writing, news reports about laws, religious discussions, or literature. In everyday speech, they would say 'break the rules' or 'cross the line'. The word is often used with 'against' or 'the boundaries of,' as in 'transgress against the community.'

distinctions.note: Violate is the everyday word for breaking a rule or law; transgress is more formal and often implies crossing a moral or social boundary.
Break is general and casual; transgress is elevated and suggests a deliberate step beyond an accepted limit.

examples.everyday: Parking in the fire lane is a clear way to transgress the rules of the building.
examples.professional: If an employee transgresses the company's data policy, HR will review the case within a week.
examples.analytical: In the Gospels, Jesus is accused of transgressing the traditions of the elders, and his response reframes what the law actually requires.

nuance.analogy: To transgress is like stepping over a painted line on a field; you go past the boundary that everyone agreed to respect.
nuance.etymology: From Latin transgredi, from trans- 'across' and gradi 'to step'; the root meaning is 'to step across'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'trans' instead of 'tranz'.
Using 'transgress' with 'to' as in 'transgress to'; the usual pattern is 'transgress against' or 'transgress the boundary'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew Scripture, the idea of transgression is often expressed by pesha', meaning rebellion or revolt against God, and in the New Testament by parabainō, meaning to step across a line or to violate a command. Matthew 15:2 uses parabainō when the scribes and Pharisees accuse the disciples of transgressing the tradition of the elders. Galatians 2:18 uses the related noun to describe a person who builds again what he has torn down and so proves himself a transgressor.

transgress.etymology: From Middle English *transgressen*, from Old French *transgresser* and Latin *transgressus*, past participle of *transgredior*.

senses.definition: The luggage storage compartment of a sedan/saloon-style car.
A storage compartment fitted behind the seat of a motorcycle.
The usually single, more or less upright part of a tree, between the roots and the branches.
In software projects under source control: the most current source tree, from which the latest unstable builds (so-called "trunk builds") are compiled.
Part of a body.
The torso; especially, the human torso.

The conspicuously extended, mobile, nose-like organ of an animal such as a sengi, a tapir or especially an elephant. The trunks of various kinds of animals might be adapted to probing and sniffing, as in the sengis, or be partly prehensile, as in the tapir, or be a versatile prehensile organ for manipulation, feeding, drinking and fighting as in the elephant.
A container.

A large suitcase, chest, or similar receptacle for carrying or storing personal possessions, usually with a hinged, often domed lid, and handles at each end, so that generally it takes two persons to carry a full trunk.
A box or chest usually covered with leather, metal, or cloth, or sometimes made of leather, hide, or metal, for holding or transporting clothes or other goods.
A channel for flow of some kind.
A major circuit between telephone switchboards or other switching equipment.
A chute or conduit, or a watertight shaft connecting two or more decks.
A long, large box, pipe, or conductor, made of plank or metal plates, for various uses, as for conveying air to a mine or to a furnace, water to a mill, grain to an elevator, etc.
A flume or sluice in which ores are separated from the slimes in which they are contained.
The main line or body of anything.
senses.example: the trunk of a vein or of an artery, as distinct from the branches

senses.definition: A main line in a river, canal, railroad, or highway system.

A large pipe forming the piston rod of a steam engine, of sufficient diameter to allow one end of the connecting rod to be attached to the crank, and the other end to pass within the pipe directly to the piston, thus making the engine more compact.
Ellipsis of swimming trunks.
The part of a pilaster between the base and capital, corresponding to the shaft of a column.
To extract (ores) from the slimes in which they are contained, by means of a trunk.
To provide simultaneous network access to multiple clients by sharing a set of circuits, carriers, channels, or frequencies.

core.definition: The enclosed storage area at the back of a car, or the main thick stem of a tree.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a clear ng followed by k. Do not insert a vowel between ng and k, and do not pronounce the final k as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain, practical word for a car part or a tree part.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say trunk for the rear storage compartment of a car, which British speakers call the boot. In casual speech, people say open the trunk or put it in the trunk. For a tree, trunk is the everyday word for the main stem; Americans also use it for an elephant's nose, but that is a specialized sense.

distinctions.note: Boot is the British term for a car's rear storage area, while Americans say trunk.
A stump is the short base left after a tree is cut down, while a trunk is the living upright stem.

examples.everyday: Can you pop the trunk so I can put these grocery bags in?
examples.professional: The trunk of our rental car had no room for the sample cases, so we rented a van.
examples.analytical: The trunk of the tree, drawing water and nutrients between root and crown, is the axis around which the whole organism is structured.

nuance.analogy: A car trunk is like a closet built into the back of a car: a closed space for things you want out of sight while you drive.
nuance.etymology: From Old French tronc, from Latin truncus, trunk or stem.
common_mistakes: Saying the boot of the car, which sounds British to Americans.
Confusing trunk with trunks, which means swimming trunks or shorts.

trunk.etymology: From Middle English *tronke*, *trunke*, from Old French *tronc* (“alms box, tree trunk, headless body”), from Latin *truncus* (“a stock, lopped tree trunk”), from *truncus* (“cut off, maimed, mutilated”).

conversation.text: Throw your suitcase in the trunk, and let's go.
Can you pop the trunk? I need to grab my jacket.
A huge tree trunk fell across the road during the storm.

senses.definition: Open all day and night, every day ("open 24 hours").

core.definition: Open all day and all night, every day of the week, without closing.

pronunciation.tip: The number is spoken with the stress on FOR and the final word on OW. In fast speech, hours often sounds like ow-erz, and the final s is a clear z.

nuance.connotation: Positive and practical. It tells customers they can come in at any time.
nuance.usage_note: In American stores, restaurants, and gyms, you will see signs that say Open 24 Hours or 24-hour service. When you ask a clerk, is it open 24 hours, a simple yes or no is a natural reply. In writing, Americans often use the numeral 24.

distinctions.note: All night describes a time period of darkness. Twenty-four hours means open at all times, including the day.
Round the clock is a common idiom that means continuously, often for people or services. Twenty-four hours is more specific and often used for stores.

examples.everyday: Is the pharmacy on Main Street open twenty-four hours, or do they close at night?
examples.professional: Our support line runs twenty-four hours, so the overnight team handles urgent tickets.
examples.analytical: A twenty-four hour service model changes how an organization thinks about staffing, fatigue, and accountability across shifts.

nuance.analogy: A twenty-four hour store is like a lighthouse that never goes dark, always ready for anyone who needs it.
nuance.etymology: Twenty-four hours is a compound of the number twenty-four and hour, from Latin hora, hour.
common_mistakes: Saying twenty four hour without the hyphen when used before a noun, as in a twenty-four-hour store.
Writing 24 hour instead of 24-hour as an adjective.

conversation.text: The pharmacy on Main Street is open twenty-four hours.
Is the grocery store open twenty-four hours, or does it close at midnight?
It's nice having a gas station that's open twenty-four hours.

senses.definition: Absolute; without conditions, limitations, reservations or qualifications.
senses.example: We demand your unconditional surrender.

senses.definition: That which is not conditional.
A conditional-like structure expressing that the consequent holds true regardless of the particular value of the antecedent.

core.definition: Absolute and not subject to any conditions, limits or exceptions, such as unconditional love or unconditional surrender.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on DISH and a lighter stress falls on the first syllable. The -tion ending is pronounced sh, and the vowels in the unstressed syllables are reduced to schwa.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, as in unconditional love or support. It is neutral in legal terms and negative in phrases such as unconditional surrender.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for love, support and forgiveness, and in news and history for unconditional surrender. In business it appears in guarantees, refunds and offers. In casual talk it expresses strong, warm commitment without strings attached.

distinctions.note: Absolute stresses totality or completeness; unconditional stresses the absence of terms or conditions attached to something.
Conditional means dependent on something else happening; unconditional is its direct opposite.

examples.everyday: My dad gave me unconditional support when I decided to change careers.
examples.professional: The vendor offered an unconditional refund within thirty days, so there was no fine print to worry about.
examples.analytical: Christian theology describes God's love as unconditional, freely given rather than earned by merit.

nuance.analogy: Like a blank check: there is no fine print and no hidden limit.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus conditional, from Latin conditio, a stipulation or agreement.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the -tion ending as tee-on; it is the sh sound, as in DISH-uh-nul.
Using the adverb unconditionally where the adjective unconditional is needed before a noun.

senses.definition: In a way that leaves no doubt; in an unequivocal or unambiguous manner, unquestionably.
senses.example: They strove to make their product unequivocally the best in the industry.

core.definition: In a clear, direct way that leaves no doubt; completely and without any hedging.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the KWIV syllable. The final -ly is an easy ee sound, and the middle syllables are quick and reduced, so don't pronounce each one fully.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It emphasizes firmness and clarity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unequivocally in news, business writing, and formal speech to show total certainty, as in The company unequivocally denied the report. In casual talk, people use totally or absolutely instead. It usually comes before the verb, which is typical of American formal style.

distinctions.note: Clearly describes how something is shown; unequivocally adds that there is no room for doubt or reinterpretation.
Absolutely is informal and emphatic in speech; unequivocally is more formal and often used for statements, denials, or endorsements.

examples.everyday: I unequivocally love this coffee shop, so we should go there again.
examples.professional: Our legal team unequivocally confirmed that the license covers commercial use.
examples.analytical: The essay unequivocally claims that moral knowledge depends on prior commitments, and it defends that claim in every section.

nuance.analogy: Like a verdict read aloud in court: once it is said clearly, it is final.
nuance.etymology: From unequivocal plus -ly, from Latin unequivocus, meaning not ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Using unequivocally in casual speech where absolutely or totally sounds more natural.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in un-ih-KWIV-uh-kuh-LEE, which makes the word sound unnatural.

senses.definition: The state of being ungodly.
Ungodly behavior.

core.definition: Behavior or attitude that shows no reverence for God; a life without respect for God's will or moral law.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GAHD, and the -iness ending is weak, so say 'nuss' rather than 'nes'. Use the American cot vowel in GAHD.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It implies serious moral or spiritual failure, often in a religious framing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use ungodliness in everyday speech. It appears in sermons, theological writing, and older or literary prose. In normal conversation people would say 'wickedness' or 'sin' instead, and it can sound stiff or preachy outside church contexts.

distinctions.note: Wickedness is general moral evil, while ungodliness specifically means lacking reverence for God.
Godlessness suggests a denial of God or indifference to religion, while ungodliness can describe a pattern of behavior that disregards God's will.

examples.everyday: My grandmother used to say that too much TV was a sign of ungodliness, though she mostly meant laziness.
examples.professional: The seminar addresses the question of how congregations respond to ungodliness in their own membership without becoming judgmental.
examples.analytical: Paul in Romans 1 treats ungodliness and unrighteousness as two linked failures, since a refusal to honor God distorts human conduct toward others.

nuance.analogy: Like a compass needle that no longer points north, the heart has lost its orientation toward God.
nuance.etymology: From Old English ungodlic, from un- (not) plus godlic, 'godly'.
common_mistakes: Using ungodliness as a casual word for bad behavior; in everyday talk people say 'bad behavior' or 'wrongdoing'.
Confusing ungodliness with godlessness; ungodliness describes behavior, while godlessness describes a lack of belief.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind ungodliness is asebeia, 'impiety' or 'irreverence toward God'. Romans 1:18 says God's wrath is revealed against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. Titus 2:12 speaks of renouncing ungodliness and worldly passions. Jude 1:15 says God will convict all the ungodly of their deeds of ungodliness.

senses.definition: Bread that is unleavened, made without a raising agent such as yeast.

core.definition: Bread made without yeast or another rising agent, eaten at Passover and used in some Christian communion traditions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'LEV' in 'unleavened', with a secondary stress on 'un'. The ending '-ened' is a weak 'und', and 'bread' has the vowel of 'bed'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to reverent, with strong religious and historical associations of haste, purity, and affliction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the phrase mostly in religious settings, especially Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. In stores, matzo is the common name for Jewish unleavened bread. 'Flatbread' is a general term.

distinctions.note: Matzo is the Jewish unleavened flatbread made under strict rules for Passover, while unleavened bread is the general category.
Flatbread is any flat bread, and may or may not be leavened, like pita or naan.
A wafer is a thin, round unleavened disc, often used for communion in Catholic and some Protestant churches.

examples.everyday: At our Seder we ate unleavened bread to remember how quickly the Israelites left Egypt.
examples.professional: I'll explain in class why Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread are linked in Exodus 12.
examples.analytical: The use of unleavened bread in the Eucharist is a point of historical difference between Eastern and Western Christianity.

nuance.analogy: Unleavened bread is bread in a hurry: no time for the dough to rise.
nuance.etymology: 'Unleavened' is un- + leavened, from leaven, from Latin levare 'to raise'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'leavened' as 'LEE-vend'.
Saying 'unleaven bread' without the -ed.
Thinking it is only a Jewish term, when Christians use it too in communion.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew matstsoth (unleavened cakes) marks Passover. Exodus 12:15-20 commands seven days of eating unleavened bread because Israel left Egypt in haste. Deuteronomy 16:3 calls it the bread of affliction. In Mark 14:12 the disciples prepare the Passover on the first day of Unleavened Bread, and 1 Corinthians 5:7-8 urges believers to celebrate with unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

traditions.view: The Byzantine Liturgy uses leavened bread (prosphora) in the Eucharist, as a sign of the living, risen Christ. Orthodox generally consider the Latin use of unleavened bread an innovation.
The Latin Church uses unleavened bread (hosts) at Mass, following the likely Passover setting of the Last Supper. Eastern Catholic churches keep leavened bread where that is their tradition.

There is no single rule. Many use ordinary leavened bread, others use wafers or unleavened bread, since Scripture does not prescribe one. Lutherans often use wafers, and many Baptist and evangelical churches use small pieces of bread or crackers.

senses.definition: Immoderate; not restrained or held in check; inordinate (literary).
senses.example: The party was a scene of unrestrained debauchery.

senses.definition: Spontaneous, natural and informal; unconstrained.
senses.example: Their meeting was one of unrestrained joy.

senses.definition: Not subject to physical restraint.

core.definition: Not held back or controlled; free, open and natural, sometimes to an excessive degree.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STRAYND, the last syllable. Say the 'str' cluster smoothly and keep the final -ed as a /d/ sound joined to the vowel, not a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Can be positive (free, spontaneous) or negative (excessive, uncontrolled), depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'unrestrained' for a joyful, uninhibited laugh or for unchecked spending or anger. Context decides the tone: 'unrestrained joy' is positive, while 'unrestrained spending' is a warning. In casual talk you might say 'she laughed without holding back.'

distinctions.note: Uncontrolled stresses lack of management; unrestrained stresses the absence of inner or outer limits, often with more energy or enthusiasm.
Unbridled is more literary and typically negative, suggesting something dangerous or wild.

examples.everyday: The kids screamed with unrestrained joy when the pool finally opened.
examples.professional: The team's unrestrained spending on software licenses needs to be reviewed before next quarter.
examples.analytical: The author treats unrestrained passion as a sign of the character's moral danger rather than his virtue.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that breaks through its banks and runs wherever it wants.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus restrained, from Latin restringere, 'to draw back or tighten'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'unrestricted', which usually refers to access or rules rather than emotion or behavior.
Using it for physical objects without restraints; 'not restrained' is clearer.

senses.definition: The period of time a computer has functioned since last requiring a reboot.
The amount of time, or the proportion of total time, during which some system or machinery is operable.

core.definition: The period during which a computer, server, or system runs and is available without failure or needing a restart.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Pronounce the second part as 'time' with a long 'i' and do not add a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is usually a positive measure when high.
nuance.usage_note: In American IT and DevOps teams, people often talk about 'uptime' as a metric, as in 'We hit 99.9 percent uptime this month.' It is almost always used in technical or business contexts. Outside work, people more often say 'it's been running fine.'

distinctions.note: 'Availability' is the formal term for the proportion of time a service is operational, while 'uptime' is the everyday technical term.
'Downtime' is the period when a system is not working; 'uptime' is the period when it is working.

examples.everyday: My laptop has been up for three weeks, so its uptime is pretty good.
examples.professional: The team committed to 99.95 percent uptime for the payment service in the new contract.
examples.analytical: A system's uptime alone does not reveal its reliability, since frequent short failures can hide behind a high average.

nuance.analogy: Like a car's odometer for time, measuring how long the engine has been running without stopping.
nuance.etymology: From 'up' plus 'time,' formed in computing in the twentieth century to describe time a machine is operating.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'uptime' as a general period of time rather than system operation.
Writing it as two words 'up time' in technical documents.

senses.definition: The message or request a user sends to a model.

core.definition: The text or question a person types into an AI model, which the model then answers or acts on.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun, the stress usually falls on 'user' with secondary stress on 'prompt,' though the phrase can sound like two equal words. The final 'er' in 'user' is a reduced r-colored vowel. The first word's stress is the one to remember.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a standard term in AI development, product work, and security reviews.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'user prompt' in software teams, AI product meetings, and security discussions to separate what a person types from the system prompt the developer writes. In casual talk people just say 'my prompt' or 'what I asked the bot.' Logging and security teams treat user prompts as untrusted input.

distinctions.note: A system prompt is written by the developer to set the model's behavior, while a user prompt is typed by the end user during the conversation.
A query usually refers to a search or database request, while a user prompt refers to natural-language input to a generative model.

collocations: prompt injection in the user prompt

examples.everyday: I typed a silly user prompt asking the chatbot for a poem about my cat, and it actually rhymed.
examples.professional: Please log each user prompt in the audit table, but mask any personal data before it reaches the analytics team.
examples.analytical: A user prompt is untrusted input, so we should treat it as a potential attack surface rather than as a trusted instruction from the developer.

nuance.analogy: A user prompt is like a customer's order slip handed to a chef, where the kitchen's house recipes are the system prompt.
nuance.etymology: 'User' comes from Middle English 'usen' (to use); 'prompt' comes from Latin promptus, 'ready, at hand,' via Middle English.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'user prompt' with 'system prompt,' which is set by the developer.
Pronouncing 'prompt' with a silent or missing 't'; the final /pt/ must be clear.

conversation.text: The user prompt is what the person actually types, as opposed to the instructions we add behind the scenes.
With consent, we log each user prompt so we can find where the assistant struggles.
Treat every user prompt as untrusted input, the same way you'd treat form data on a website.

senses.definition: An exorbitant rate of interest, in excess of any legal rates or at least immorally.

core.definition: The practice of lending money at interest rates that are excessively high, illegal, or morally unacceptable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with 'zh' as in 'measure' in the middle. The final syllables are reduced: 'uh-ree,' with the r rhotic. Do not say 'yoo-SURE-ee.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies greed or exploitation of borrowers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'usury' mainly in legal history, religious discussion, economics, and literature such as Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice. In everyday speech they say 'loan shark' or 'predatory lending.' Legal limits on interest are called 'usury laws' in the United States, and they vary by state.

distinctions.note: 'Interest' is the normal payment for borrowing money, while 'usury' refers to excessive or illegal interest.
A 'loan shark' is a person who lends illegally at high rates, while 'usury' is the act or concept of excessive lending.

examples.everyday: My uncle warned me to avoid that lender, because the rates sound like pure usury.
examples.professional: Our compliance team checks state usury laws before we approve any high-rate consumer loan.
examples.analytical: Medieval theologians condemned usury because they saw the charging of interest on loans as exploiting the need of the borrower.

nuance.analogy: Like a fee on a bank that keeps growing until the borrower owes more than they ever received.
nuance.etymology: From Latin usura, 'interest on a loan,' from usus, 'use.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'usury' with 'usurp,' which means to seize power.
Using 'usury' for ordinary, legal interest; it implies an excessive or unlawful rate.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word neshek, 'bite,' is used for interest in Exodus 22:25, where Israelites are told not to charge interest to fellow poor people. Leviticus 25:36-37 forbids taking interest from a poor brother, while Deuteronomy 23:19-20 allows interest from foreigners but not from fellow Israelites. The laws show concern for the vulnerable and for mutual support within the community.

traditions.view: The Orthodox Church has historically condemned usury, following the Old Testament and early church councils, and has treated excessive interest on loans to the poor as a moral wrong.
The Catholic Church historically condemned usury as the charging of any interest on loans, but modern teaching distinguishes exploitative lending from fair interest in economic life.

Protestants, following Calvin, generally allowed moderate interest on commercial loans while condemning exploitation of the poor; Lutherans and Reformed Christians differ on how strictly to apply these limits.

usury.etymology: From Middle English *usurie*, from Latin *ūsūria*, from *ūsūra* (“lending at interest, usury”) from *ūsus* (“use”), from stem of *utor* (“to use”).

senses.definition: A referential book such as a handbook or manual, especially one that is pocketable.
A useful object, constantly carried on one's person.

core.definition: A small handbook or guidebook that you carry with you for constant reference.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second word, 'MEE', with a lighter stress on 'vay'. Americans usually say 'vay-dee' rather than the Latin 'WAH-day'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests a useful, trusted companion book, but it sounds bookish.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'vade mecum' in academic or literary writing, not in everyday speech. Everyday speakers say 'handbook', 'guide' or 'go-to book' instead. It is a Latin phrase, so it can sound a bit showy in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: A handbook is the common everyday word for a practical guide, while vade mecum is a more formal and literary term for a book kept at hand.
A manual gives step-by-step instructions for a task, while a vade mecum is a broader reference book carried for regular use.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's old cookbook is my vade mecum in the kitchen.
examples.professional: This API guide has become our vade mecum for onboarding new engineers.
examples.analytical: Aquinas's Summa served generations of scholars as a vade mecum of theological reasoning.

nuance.analogy: A vade mecum is like a pocket map you never leave home without.
nuance.etymology: Latin, literally 'go with me'.
common_mistakes: Writing it as one word or spelling 'vademecum' in formal work; it is two words in standard English.
Pronouncing it as a Latin phrase with 'WAH-day MAY-koom' in everyday American speech.

senses.definition: An elongated depression cast between hills or mountains, often with a river flowing through it.
senses.example: The Indus River valley was the site of an ancient civilization.

senses.definition: An area which drains itself into a river.
Any structure resembling one, e.g. the interior angle formed by the intersection of two sloping roof planes.
(rare, poetic) To form the shape of a valley.
senses.label: rare, poetic

core.definition: A low stretch of land between hills or mountains, often with a river or stream running through it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final 'ey' is a light 'ee', and the word has only two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It often evokes rural landscapes, farms, or scenic beauty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'valley' in everyday conversation for places such as the San Fernando Valley or the Napa Valley. It is common in travel talk, weather reports, and descriptions of geography. 'Valley' is also used figuratively for a low point, as in 'valley of despair'.

distinctions.note: A canyon is a deep, steep-sided valley usually cut by a river over a long time. A valley is generally wider and gentler.
A basin is a low area with no outlet for water to drain away. A valley usually has a river or stream flowing through it.

examples.everyday: We drove through the valley on our way to the lake, and the fall colors were beautiful.
examples.professional: The construction crew had to reroute the road because the valley floods every spring.
examples.analytical: Many Psalms describe the valley as a place of danger, which later readers often interpret as a picture of human mortality.

nuance.analogy: A valley is like the low part of a bowl between two raised edges, with water tending to collect in the middle.
nuance.etymology: From Old French val, from Latin vallis.
common_mistakes: Using 'valley' for any low spot; it normally means a land feature between hills or mountains.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a full 'lay' rather than a light 'ee'.

valley.etymology: From Middle English *valeye*, *valey*, from Anglo-Norman *valey*, Old French *valee*, from Latin *vallēs*/*vallis*.

conversation.text: The whole valley gets foggy in the morning.
We camped down in the valley next to the river.
From up here you can see the entire valley.

senses.definition: Manly; having characteristics associated with being male, such as strength; exhibiting masculine traits to an exaggerated degree such as strength, forcefulness or vigor.
Pertaining to a grammatical gender used in plurals of some Slavic languages, corresponding to the personal masculine animate nouns.
Possessing high sexual drive and capacity for sexual intercourse.

core.definition: Having the strength, energy and vigor traditionally associated with men, or sexually vigorous.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, 'VIR'. The second syllable is weak, and the r is pronounced clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Often positive in describing physical strength, but it can sound old-fashioned or sexist and can suggest exaggerated masculinity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'virile' in writing, reviews or descriptions of a man's strength or energy. In casual talk, people more often say 'strong' or 'masculine', and the word can sound dated or condescending if used about a real person. Use it carefully, since sexual meanings can be misread.

distinctions.note: 'Manly' is a common, everyday word for typical male qualities, while 'virile' is more formal and emphasizes strength or sexual vigor.
'Masculine' describes typical traits or features of men in general, while 'virile' highlights strength or energy, sometimes to an exaggerated degree.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a retired firefighter, and he still has a virile energy that shocks people half his age.
examples.professional: The marketing team thought the new ad campaign looked too virile and decided to soften the message.
examples.analytical: The poet connects virile courage with political power, which shows how ancient ideals of manhood still shape modern notions of leadership.

nuance.analogy: A virile man is like an old oak tree: strong and sturdy, with a strength people notice from far away.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'virilis' (of a man), from 'vir' (man).
common_mistakes: Using 'virile' as a casual synonym for 'manly' in everyday compliments, which can sound odd or inappropriate.
Stressing the second syllable, 'vih-RILE', which is a common error.

virile.etymology: From Middle French *viril*, from Latin *virīlis*, from *vir* + *īlis*.

senses.definition: A solemn promise to perform some act, or behave in a specified manner, especially a promise to live and act in accordance with the rules of a religious order.
senses.example: The old hermit, up in the mountains, took a vow of silence.

senses.definition: A declaration or assertion.
To make a vow; to promise.
To make a vow regarding (something).
senses.example: The wronged woman vowed revenge.

senses.definition: To declare publicly that one has made a vow, usually to show one's determination or to announce an act of retaliation.
senses.example: The rebels vowed to continue their fight.

core.definition: A serious promise to do something or to behave in a certain way, often made to God or to a person.

pronunciation.tip: The 'ow' is the diphthong of 'how' and 'now'. Do not pronounce it like 'vo' in 'vote'. The final sound is a clear, long diphthong.

nuance.connotation: Positive or serious; it suggests commitment and sincerity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'vow' most often in wedding, religious or formal promise contexts, such as 'marriage vows'. In casual talk, people say 'promise' or 'swear'. 'I vow' can sound dramatic but is natural when joking about a firm resolution.

distinctions.note: 'Promise' is everyday and flexible; 'vow' is more solemn and formal.
An oath is a formal statement, often legal or public; a vow is a personal solemn promise.
A pledge can be public or financial and less intimate; a vow is more personal or religious.

examples.everyday: I made a vow to stop eating junk food, but I already broke it at lunch.
examples.professional: I vow to deliver the revised report by Friday, even if I need to work late.
examples.analytical: In the biblical tradition, a vow is a binding promise to God, and breaking it carries serious moral weight.

nuance.analogy: A vow is like a rope tied to your word; once tied, it holds you to your promise.
nuance.etymology: From Latin votum, 'a wish or solemn promise'.
common_mistakes: Using 'vow' as a casual word for every small promise; 'promise' is more natural.
Pronouncing it like 'vote' with a short 'o'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word neder means a vow made to God. Numbers 30:2 (RSV) says that a man who vows a vow to the LORD must not break his word. Deuteronomy 23:21 instructs that a vow to God must be paid without delay. Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 warns that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.

traditions.view: Monastic vows of poverty, chastity and obedience are made at tonsure and are seen as a lifelong dedication to the ascetic life within the Church.
Religious vows are public, binding promises recognized in canon law, and marriage vows are a sacrament.
Most Protestants do not take monastic vows and view personal vows as serious promises, though some Anglican and Lutheran communities keep vows, and marriage vows are not sacramental.

vow.etymology: Middle English *vowe*, *voue*, that from Old French *vut*, in turn from Latin *vōtum* (“a promise, dedication, vow”), from *voveo* (“to promise, vow”).

senses.definition: A weakness which allows an attacker to reduce a system's security.
The state of being vulnerable; susceptibility to attack or injury, either physical or emotional; the state or condition of being weak or poorly defended.
senses.example: The country recognized their defense vulnerability after an airplane landed in front of the central square without any consequences.

senses.definition: A specific weakness in the protections or defences that (literally or figuratively) surround someone or something.

core.definition: The state of being open to attack, harm, or injury, or a specific weakness that makes someone or something easier to attack or damage.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'BIL,' and the middle syllables reduce to a quick 'nuh' or 'ruh.' Many learners over-pronounce the 'ra' or 'ti' endings; keep the final syllable short as 'tee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical contexts such as security reports, but often negative or sensitive when used about people's emotional or physical state.
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces, 'vulnerability' is standard in cybersecurity, risk management, and software discussions, where a 'vulnerability' is a flaw in code or systems. In personal conversation, Americans use it for emotional openness, as in 'showing vulnerability,' which is often seen positively in leadership and friendship. For casual talk about being weak or exposed, 'weak spot' or 'sore spot' often sounds more natural.

distinctions.note: Susceptibility is a general tendency to be affected by something, such as a susceptibility to colds, while vulnerability emphasizes exposure to a specific threat or attack.
A weakness is any shortcoming, whereas a vulnerability is specifically a weakness that could be exploited or harmed by an attacker or a threat.

examples.everyday: My neighbor said that being open about her divorce made her feel a lot of vulnerability, but it also brought her closer to her friends.
examples.professional: The security team found a vulnerability in the login module, so we patched it before the next release.
examples.analytical: Christian anthropology has often treated human vulnerability not as a defect but as the condition in which dependence on God and on others becomes visible.

nuance.analogy: A vulnerability is like an unlocked back door in a house: the walls may be strong, but one unguarded entrance is enough for an intruder.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'vulnerabilis,' from Latin 'vulnerare,' to wound, from 'vulnus,' wound.
common_mistakes: Saying 'vulnerablity' by dropping the second 'a' sound; the word has the full 'vul-ner-a-bil-i-ty' sequence.
Using 'vulnerability' for a single bad habit; in American usage it usually names a specific exposure or weakness.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible does not use the English word 'vulnerability,' but it expresses the idea of human frailty and dependence. In 2 Corinthians 12:9, Paul says that God's power is made perfect in weakness, a passage often cited in discussions of human vulnerability. The Greek word 'asthenia' (weakness) is used there, and it refers to human limitation that makes room for grace.

senses.definition: Authorization or certification; a sanction, as given by a superior.
Something that provides assurance or confirmation; a guarantee or proof.
senses.example: a warrant of authenticity; a warrant for success

senses.definition: An order that serves as authorization; especially a voucher authorizing payment or receipt of money.
An option, usually issued together with another security and with a term at issue greater than a year, to buy other securities of the issuer.
Ellipsis of warrant officer.
A certificate of appointment given to a warrant officer.
Underclay in a coal mine.
A judicial writ authorizing an officer to make a search, seizure, or arrest, or to execute a judgment.
senses.example: an arrest warrant issued by the court

senses.definition: To guarantee (something) to be (of a specified quality, value, etc.).
To guarantee as being true; to believe strongly.
senses.example: That tree is going to fall, I’ll warrant.

senses.definition: To authorize; to give (someone) sanction or warrant (to do something).
senses.example: I am warranted to search these premises fully.

senses.definition: To justify; to give grounds for.
senses.example: Circumstances arose that warranted the use of lethal force.

core.definition: An official document from a judge authorizing police to arrest someone or search a place; also a good reason that justifies a belief or action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and the second syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'WOR-unt', not 'war-RANT'. The r is clear, and the final t is often very light.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In legal contexts it is serious and formal; in philosophy and argument it simply means justification.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear warrant in news about police, such as 'The officers had a search warrant.' In everyday speech, people more often say 'no reason to' or 'justified.' In academic or philosophical writing, 'warrant' names what justifies believing a claim, as in 'What warrant do we have for this conclusion?'

distinctions.note: License is official permission to do an activity, while warrant is a specific document or justification for a particular action.
Reason is any explanation; warrant is stronger and usually implies official authority or solid grounds.

examples.everyday: The police showed up with an arrest warrant, and my neighbor was shocked.
examples.professional: Before we change the pricing model, we need enough data to warrant the risk.
examples.analytical: Reformed epistemologists argue that belief in God can have its own warrant without depending on inference from other premises.

nuance.analogy: A warrant is like a permission slip with a judge's signature: it gives official grounds for acting.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French 'warant', meaning guarantee or protection, from Germanic roots.
common_mistakes: Using 'warrant' for ordinary reasons in casual talk, which can sound too legal.
Confusing the noun 'warrant' with 'warranty', which is a product guarantee.

will-i-get-my-security-deposit-back.phonetic: /wɪl aɪ ˌɡɛt maɪ sɪˌkjʊɹəti dəˌpɑzɪt ˈbæk/

senses.definition: Asking whether the landlord will return your deposit when you move out; by law it comes back minus any damage beyond normal wear and tear.

core.definition: A question asking whether your landlord will return your rental deposit when you move out, minus any damage costs.

pronunciation.respelling: wil eye get mye sih-KYOOR-ih-tee dih-PAH-zit BAK
pronunciation.tip: 'Security' is stressed on KYOOR, and 'deposit' on PAH. The t in 'security' is flapped, so it sounds almost like a d. In 'get back' the main stress falls on 'back'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, with some anxiety, since it concerns money.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this when moving out or signing a lease. Deadlines and rules vary by state, and landlords usually must itemize any deductions and may not charge for normal wear and tear. A typical reply is 'Yes, if you leave it clean and undamaged, and give me your forwarding address.'

distinctions.note: A security deposit is refundable if the unit is left in good condition; an application fee usually is not.
A down payment is part of the purchase price of a home; a security deposit is held as protection and returned under the lease terms.

examples.everyday: Will we get our security deposit back if we leave the place spotless?
examples.professional: Before we sign, will I get my security deposit back if we end the sublease early?
examples.analytical: Whether a tenant recovers a security deposit depends on the lease terms and on state law distinguishing damage from normal wear and tear.

nuance.analogy: Like a library book deposit: you pay up front, and you get it back if you return the item in good condition.
nuance.etymology: 'Security' comes from Latin securitas ('freedom from care'); 'deposit' comes from Latin depositum ('something entrusted'), from deponere ('put down').
common_mistakes: Stressing 'deposit' on the first syllable; it is stressed on the second, dih-PAH-zit.
Confusing a security deposit with a down payment or an application fee.

conversation.text: We cleaned everything and patched the nail holes. Will I get my security deposit back?
If I break the lease early, will I get my security deposit back?

senses.definition: To shrivel, droop or dry up, especially from lack of water.
senses.example: The flowers began to wither in the hot sun without enough water.

senses.definition: To cause to shrivel or dry up.
To lose vigor or power; to languish; to waste away; to pass away.
To become helpless due to emotion.
To make helpless due to emotion.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

senses.definition: To go against, resist; oppose.
Singular of withers (“part of the back of a four-legged animal that is between the shoulder blades”)

core.definition: To shrivel, droop, or dry up, often from lack of water, heat, or care.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and voice the 'th' as in 'with'. The final 'er' is a reduced American r-colored vowel, not a full 'ur' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests decline, loss of life, or weakening, though it can be used for dramatic or figurative effect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wither' for plants, and also figuratively for hopes, relationships, or a person's health. In everyday speech they more often say 'wilt' for plants or 'dry up' and 'fade', so 'wither' sounds more literary. Describing a withering look or a withering critique is common in writing and criticism.
word_family: withers (noun, the shoulder ridge of a horse)

distinctions.note: 'Wilt' usually describes plants losing firmness and drooping, while 'wither' covers a broader drying up or decline, including figurative uses.
'Fade' refers to color or intensity lessening, while 'wither' implies life or strength being drained away.

examples.everyday: If you forget to water the tomatoes this week, they'll wither in the heat.
examples.professional: Without budget support, the pilot program will wither before the end of the fiscal year.
examples.analytical: Liberal theologians worried that a faith reduced to ritual would wither into empty habit.

nuance.analogy: Withering is like a balloon slowly losing air: the shape remains for a while, but the life inside gradually drains away.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English widderen, related to 'with' in the sense of 'against', so originally 'to turn away or resist'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'th' as /θ/ as in 'thin'; in 'wither' it is the voiced sound.
Using 'wither' for ordinary daily tiredness, where it sounds too dramatic.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Greek New Testament the verb xēraino means 'to dry up' or 'to wither', and it describes plants and the fig tree losing life. Psalm 1:3 describes the righteous person as a tree planted by water whose leaf does not wither, contrasting stable faith with the fate of the wicked. Mark 11:20 reports that the fig tree Jesus cursed had withered away when the disciples passed it the next morning. Isaiah 40:7-8 says that the grass withers and the flower fades, while the word of God stands forever.

wither.etymology: From Middle English *widren*, *wydderen* (“to dry up, shrivel”), related to or perhaps an alteration of Middle English *wederen* (“to expose to weather”), from Old English *wederian* (“to expose to weather, exhibit a change of weather”).

senses.definition: One who hates or fears strangers or foreigners.

core.definition: A person who strongly dislikes, fears, or distrusts foreigners or people from other groups.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ZEN. The final syllable rhymes with 'robe,' so end with a clear b sound, not a p.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; calling someone a xenophobe is a serious criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'xenophobe' in political, social, or news discussions about prejudice. Calling a person a xenophobe in conversation is a strong insult and can cause conflict. Use it carefully, and prefer describing behavior when possible.

distinctions.note: Racist refers to beliefs or actions based on race; xenophobe focuses on fear or hatred of outsiders or foreigners in general.
Bigot is a broader insult for someone intolerant of any group; xenophobe is narrower.

collocations: accuse someone of being a xenophobe

examples.everyday: My uncle gets angry about immigrants, and my sister says he is basically a xenophobe.
examples.professional: Several reviewers said the manager's comments made him sound like a xenophobe, so HR is looking into it.
examples.analytical: Labeling a critic as a xenophobe can end debate before the substantive policy argument begins.

nuance.analogy: A xenophobe is like someone who locks the door whenever a stranger knocks, assuming every visitor is a threat.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'xenos,' stranger, and 'phobos,' fear.
common_mistakes: Using 'xenophobe' as a casual term for someone who is shy with strangers.
Spelling it with a c or misplacing the stress.
